_source.Title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
_source.Keywords: Cool Flames     thermo-convective perturbation     Droplet combustion     FLEX
_source.Proposal Title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI grant
_source.Objectives: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
_source.Approach:
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
_source.Hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

_source.Title: Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures
_source.Keywords: Microgravity     Dendritic structure     dendritic arm     Interfacial Shape Distribution     Phase Field Modeling
_source.Proposal Title: Coarsening of Dendritic Solid-Liquid Mixtures
_source.Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to study dendritic coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid. Specific interest was in examining dendritic structure close to the dendrite tip. Additional objectives included measuring the rate at which topological singularities  occur when a secondary dendrite arm separates from the main dendrite stem or when two arms fuse together.
_source.Approach: The CSLM-3 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM and CSLM-2 investigations. The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn samples for CSLM-3 were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 48 hours were employed. After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas. Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure. The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system. The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment.
_source.Hypothesis:
The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows:
Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite? If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening? How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure? How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system? How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system? Does scaling exist?
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. This investigation will provide insights into the dynamics of dendritic morphological evolution and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process and validating them using benchmark experimental data is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

_source.Title: Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data
_source.Keywords: PSI Grant     numerical method     heat transfer rate     moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure     multi-material systems     complex boundaries     discontinuous diffusion coefficients
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.
_source.Approach:
The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell. The salient features of the overall approach includes:
(i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii)  the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces,  a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will  straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse. It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics. In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors. The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices.

_source.Title: Capillary Flow Experiment - 2
_source.Keywords: CFE     Capillary forces     Capillary Flow Experiment (CFE)     CFE-2
_source.Objectives: Liquids behave differently in space than they do on Earth, so containers that can process, hold or transport them must be designed carefully to work in microgravity. The Capillary Flow Experiment-2 furthers research on wetting, which is a liquid’s ability to spread across a surface, and its impact over large length scales in strange container shapes in microgravity environments. This work will improve our capabilities to quickly and accurately predict how related processes occur, and allow us to design better systems to process liquids aboard spacecraft (i.e., liquid fuel tanks, thermals fluids, and water processing for life support).
_source.Approach: Wetting describes how well a liquid is attracted to a solid surface. Understanding the impact of wetting over large length scales in microgravity is important for a wide variety of engineering systems being developed for human spaceflight.Studies from CFE-2 may serve to demonstrate how liquids can be efficiently and passively separated from gases in the absence of gravity. This is a key operation in fluid systems aboard spacecraft such as water purification systems for life support.
_source.Hypothesis: This research hypothesizes that capillary flows in microgravity are strongly influenced by container geometry, particularly interior corners and gaps. For vane gaps, a critical wetting condition, dependent on gap size and vane design, is expected. In interior corners, imbibition rates, phase separation, and bubble dynamics should be highly sensitive to 3D geometry, with long-duration microgravity being crucial for observing subtle, slow processes. Experiments are designed to quantify these relationships and validate theoretical models.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The Capillary Flow Experiments demonstrate how capillary forces work in space, how differently shaped containers change the wicking behavior of a wetting fluid, and how such can be used to passively separate liquids and gases.  Understanding how microgravity amplifies these behaviors could improve the reliability of such key processes as water purification fuel storage and supply, and general liquid transport aboard spacecraft. On Earth capillary action allows small amounts of liquid to flow up and into tight spaces despite the effects of gravity. New miniature medical devices, known as lab-on-a-chip technologies, exploit this phenomenon to draw blood or other fluids into essentially miniature l diagnostic systems. CFE-2 improves our understanding of how capillary forces work in a variety of system geometries including the open spaces within porous materials such as sand and soil, wicks and sponges.

_source.Title: Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures
_source.Keywords: solidification     Soldering     Micromechanical Testing     Extreme Temperatures     Marangoni Convection     Microstructure Characterization     Porosity
_source.SubResearch Area: Microstructural Characterization, Terrestrial vs Microgravity Effects, Solder Joints
_source.Proposal Title: Structure, Properties, and Performance of Solder Joints in Terrestrial vs. Reduced-Gravity Environments
_source.Objectives: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.
_source.Approach:
The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu.
Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.
_source.Hypothesis: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives:

(i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.

_source.Title: Packed Bed Reactor Experiment
_source.Keywords: PBRE-WR     PBRE-2     PBRE     Packed Bed Reactors
_source.Objectives: The PBRE studies the behavior of gases and liquids when they flow simultaneously through a column filled with fixed porous media. The porous media or “packing” can be made of different shapes and materials and are used widely in chemical engineering as a means to enhance the contact between two immiscible fluid phases (e.g., liquid-gas, water-oil, etc.). Packed columns can serve as reactors, scrubbers, strippers, etc. in systems where efficient interphase contact is desired, both on Earth and in space.
_source.Approach:
The PBRE investigation employs an approach that combines theoretical modeling with rigorous experimental testing to achieve its objectives. Here's a breakdown of the key aspects:

1. Theoretical Modeling:

Existing Models: PBRE builds upon existing models for pressure drop and flow regime transitions in packed bed reactors, particularly those developed by Motil et al. (2003) and Guo et al. (2004).

Model Validation: The experiment focuses on validating these models, extending them to lower flow rates relevant to water recovery systems, and bridging them with other models.

New Models: The data collected through PBRE is used to develop new models and scaling laws that accurately predict flow characteristics in 0-g and partial-g environments.

2. Experimental Setup and Procedures:

Test Sections: PBRE utilizes two identical test sections, each a 60 cm long, 5 cm diameter cylindrical column. One section is packed with glass beads (wetting), the other with Teflon beads (non-wetting) to isolate surface tension effects.

Fluid Flow: The experiment uses nitrogen and water as the gas and liquid phases, with a wide range of flow rates, from very low to high, to cover operational regimes.

Instrumentation: A comprehensive suite of sensors is used to measure flow rates, temperatures, and pressures. The experiment also includes two high-speed video cameras to visualize flow patterns.

Test Matrix: The investigation is organized into several test series (''Ops''), each focused on specific flow conditions and packing materials.

Data Acquisition: The experiment meticulously collects data, with careful time-correlation of measurements to ensure accurate analysis.

3. Addressing Anomalies:

Flow Rate Control: The team encountered anomalies with the GN2 flow rate and pressure fluctuations, leading to troubleshooting and adjustments in the experiment's setup and procedures.

High-Speed Video: The cameras experienced limitations with operating at the desired frame rates, requiring modifications to data acquisition strategies.

4. Data Analysis:

Model Validation: Data is analyzed to compare experimental results with model predictions, identifying any discrepancies and refining the models.

New Model Development: The collected data is used to develop new models and scaling laws, aiming for greater accuracy and applicability in microgravity environments.

5. Data Organization:

Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): The PBRE team meticulously organizes the experimental data in PSI, a database for physical sciences data, to ensure accessibility and analysis.

The PBRE investigation relies on a combination of theoretical modeling, rigorous experimental testing, and comprehensive data analysis to achieve its objectives. This approach is designed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of packed bed reactors in microgravity, leading to improved design tools and operational strategies for future space applications.

6. Dissemination of Results:

The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through:

Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community.

Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops.

Reports and documentation: Preparing detailed reports and documentation of the experimental procedures, data analysis, and conclusions.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the gravity plays a significant role in determining the flow characteristics (pressure drop, flow regime transitions, liquid holdup, and mass transfer) of gas-liquid flows through porous media.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Water-recovery systems, fuel cells and other equipment on the International Space Station use packed bed reactors, but currently none are designed to handle both liquid and gas at the same time. With improved understanding of how packed bed two-phase flow works in microgravity, scientists are be able to design more efficient, lightweight thermal management and life support systems that use less energy, benefiting the Space Station and future lunar and Mars missions. Design rules for gas-liquid flows through packed columns are well developed on Earth (i.e., for normal gravity) but lacking for reduced or zero gravity. The Packed Bed Reactor Experiment seeks to fill this knowledge gap by studying the hydrodynamics of gas-liquid flows in zero gravity through packed columns. By understanding how gravity affects gas-liquid flows through packed columns (or packed beds, as they are known in the industry) better, more predictive correlations for pressure drops and flow regime maps can be developed with the proper gravity-dependent terms included.

_source.Title: Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-1
_source.Keywords: Colloids     magnetorheological (MR) fluid     microgravity
_source.Objectives: InSPACE-1 studied the response of MR fluids under continuous and pulsed magnetic fields in a microgravity environment.  An objective was to determine the true three-dimensional low-energy (equilibrium) structure of an magneto-rheological (MR) emulsion in a pulsed magnetic field. InSPACE-1 aimed to conduct a microscopic video study of the MR fluid in a pulsed magnetic field to determine the effect of varying magnetic field, pulse frequency, and particle size on the equilibrium microstructures. A pulsed magnetic field is used to mimic the forces applied to these fluids in real applications, such as vibration damping systems. A pulsed field also tends to produce intricate, thick structures with different properties than structures produced by a constant magnetic field.
_source.Approach: The MR samples for InSPACE-1 were ferrofluid emulsions consisting of iron oxide nanoparticles suspended in a solution of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, an anionic surfactant), and ultrapure water. These samples were comprised of uniform particles sizes of 0.31, 0.40, and 0.66 μm and volume fraction 2 percent. The parameters varied during the series of tests were the field strength, the particle size, and the pulse frequency. During experimental runs the Lightbox Assembly provided the backlighting source to illuminate the samples. The InSPACE Avionics Assembly was used to output an electrical current and frequency that could be adjusted to produce a pulsed-magnetic field inside the Helmholtz coil. This magnetic field caused the particles in the fluid to group together, or aggregate, and form microstructures inside the fluid. A camera was used to record the display on the avionic assembly. The Optics Assembly was composed of two cameras with optic lens for a right angle view and a straight view of the sample. A Helmholtz coil was mounted on the optic assembly and housed the InSPACE-1 sample. For InSPACE-1, the Helmholtz Coil Assembly (CA) and the sample Vial Assemblies were integrated as a single unit.
_source.Hypothesis: The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces. In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: MR fluids can quickly transition into a nearly solid-like state when exposed to a magnetic field and return to their original liquid state when the magnetic field is removed. Their relative stiffness can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the magnetic field. Due to the rapid-response interface that they provide between mechanical components and electronic controls, for terrestrial applications MR fluids can be used to improve or develop new brake systems, seat suspensions, robotics, clutches, airplane landing gear, and active damping systems for bridges (to counter act wind gusts) and buildings. For space exploration the results will lead to MR applications for limb and dextrous motion in robotic components and human-robotic interfaces for EVA suits.

_source.Title: Cold Atom Lab - Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-Geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates
_source.Keywords: Bose-Einstein Condensates     Rf/microwave dressing potentials     Bubble Topology     Vortex Physics
_source.Objectives: Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates (Cold Atom Lab - BEC Bubble Dynamics) aims to study Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) and degenerate Fermi gases (DFGs) confined to a the surface of an experimentally-controlled topologically-connected ''bubble.'' The limitations of gravitational sag have prevented terrestrial exploration of a quantum gas confined to such as surface. This investigation aims to test fundamental ideas in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and strongly-correlated many-body physics in condensed matter. Studying the behavior of quantum gas bubbles could provide insights for next-generation quantum sensors and simulators.
_source.Approach:
This investigation uses rubidium (87 Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations.

Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas:
    Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned.
    State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region.
    Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures.
    Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases.

Manipulation and Probing:
    Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements.
    Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample.

The manipulation and probing aspect is particularly important for this specific investigation as the ultracold atomic gas must be treated with certain fields to achieve the bubble topology. To do this, a locally harmonic spin-dependent trapping potential originating from inside an applied magnetic field is combined with a near-resonance oscillatory magnetic field with a certain radiofrequency. Together these two magnetic fields produce atoms in spatially dependent dressed atomic states that experience dressed or adiabatic dressed potentials. These potentials can then be manipulated via tuning the radiofrequency field so that the atoms take on an ellipsoid or bubble-like geometry.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that radiofrequency dressing can be used to create a trap formed by a spherical or ellipsoidal shell structure capable of confining quantum gases to a “bubble” topology. Due to gravitational sag and trap distortion present in terrestrial experiments this trap topology has not been explored, and further, it is only able to be explored in the microgravity environment unique to the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL). The low-energy excitations of such systems, as well as various theories on the physics of phase transitions will be investigated using this bubble-geometry.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This work, while focused on the fundamental physics of ultracold atoms and not directly connected to human life, has a similar impact to life on Earth as that of all fundamental physics; it broadens our understanding of the physical world and helps us further cement our collective picture of quantum mechanics as ''the way the world works.'' It explores the limits of how large Bose-Einstein condensates can be made, and to what extent the gravity-well of terrestrial labs render certain investigations difficult or impossible. The observations made aboard CAL through this project are a clear demonstration that physical insight can sometimes require microgravity facilities to be fully developed, and that space borne atomic physics experiments can be valuable contributions to our collective scientific efforts. Additionally, insight into fundamental laws of quantum mechanics can have many applications in many on Earth. Quantum computers continue to exponentially accelerate as a field of study and in industry, and research into these fundamentals can support scientific workforce development, public science outreach and research and development.

_source.Title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
_source.Keywords: SAME Data     Nanoparticles     Ground-based research     Dibutyl pthalate     thermophoresis     Aerosol Smoke Generation     Navier-Stokes nodal approach     Numerical Simulation     Particle settling
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI Grant
_source.Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
_source.Approach: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined.  Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.
_source.Hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

_source.Title: Binary Colloidal Alloy Test - 3
_source.Keywords: Colloids     microgravity     Polymers     phase separation
_source.Proposal Title: Dynamics and Structure in Colloidal Suspensions Far from Equilibrium
_source.Objectives:
The BCAT-3 investigation aimed to exploit the long range ordered structures formed using the self-assembly of colloidal particles and demonstrate the use of colloid engineering to synthesize new materials with novel properties. The goal was to use a mixture of two different materials or binary alloys to greatly increase the flexibility of the resultant colloidal structures and qualitatively study the phase behavior and crystallization properties of these binary alloys. In addition, the investigation proposed to study the properties of mixtures of colloids and polymers where the addition of the polymer induces weak attractive interactions between the colloidal particles by the depletion mechanism, leading to a rich phase behavior for the colloidal
particles.
_source.Approach: BCAT-3 is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS.  The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells. The ten samples in BCAT-3 were selected as part of three separate experiments examining different physical processes: critical point, binary alloys, and surface crystallization. The samples were manually homogenized using a stir-bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette.  Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.
_source.Hypothesis: Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Self-assembly of micron and submicron colloidal particles into highly ordered three-dimensional structures offers an alternative to traditional lithographic techniques, which are often limited to surface-level patterning. These ordered arrays of particles can exhibit novel optical properties, such as redirecting light via diffraction or altering local photon densities, enabling the creation of advanced optical filters, switches, and sensors. Moreover, these structures can serve as templates for macroporous materials, which have diverse chemical applications, including catalysis, separation media, and biomaterials. Precision macroporous ceramics and polymers can also be used as lightweight insulators, chromatographic materials, and catalytic supports, offering transformative solutions across industries such as energy, manufacturing, and medicine.

_source.Title: Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories
_source.Keywords: Rheology     Viscoelastic Suspensions     Particle–Polymer Interactions     SHERE
_source.Proposal Title: Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the dynamic rheology of particle-filled polymeric fluids in complex flows. These fluids, encountered in manufacturing processes such as fiber spinning, hydraulic fracturing, and roll-to-roll film production, experience alternating regimes of shear and extension in a Lagrangian frame. By using SHERE’s microgravity dataset, the study seeks to isolate the interplay between polymer stresses, particle orientation, and flow disturbances—effects that cannot be cleanly separated in Earth’s gravity. The overarching goal is to develop quantitative predictions and mechanistic insights into how particles alter extensional flow responses, strain hardening, and energy dissipation in viscoelastic suspensions.
_source.Approach: The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation. The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions in Boger fluids at moderate extension rates—regimes inaccessible on Earth due to sedimentation and buoyancy. To interpret these data, the project applies finite-difference methods in spheroidal coordinates to resolve inertia-less viscoelastic flows around suspended particles, capturing strong local stress gradients near particle surfaces. Semi-analytical theories are also employed to predict rheology in the limit of small polymer concentrations, allowing parameter sweeps that are computationally prohibitive in full simulations. Three flow classes are studied: (1) sphere suspensions in transient extension with/without pre-shear to directly compare with SHERE data; (2) spheroidal particle suspensions transitioning between shear and extension to mimic fiber-film processing; and (3) alternating shear/extension flows modeling turbulent drag reduction. Together, this multi-method approach bridges PSI experimental data with first-principles rheological predictions.
_source.Hypothesis: The central hypothesis is that particle-polymer interactions fundamentally alter the transient extensional rheology of polymer solutions in ways that cannot be predicted by simple additive models of particle and polymer stresses. Specifically, the particle-induced velocity disturbances are expected to modify local polymer stress distributions, suppress strain hardening at large deformations, and alter stress development depending on flow history (e.g., pre-shear orientation effects). Furthermore, anisotropic particles such as spheroids will introduce orientation-dependent rheological signatures, leading to different stress responses under alternating shear and extension. By validating these predictions with SHERE microgravity data, the study tests whether advanced numerical and theoretical models can accurately capture the coupled dynamics of particles and polymers across relevant industrial flow regimes.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
In-Space Benefits: For space exploration and on-orbit manufacturing, understanding the rheology of particle-laden polymeric fluids is crucial for the design of efficient life-support systems, in-space fabrication, and thermal management technologies. Microgravity eliminates sedimentation, enabling stable suspensions and novel material processing methods, such as fiber spinning and advanced coatings. Insights from SHERE-based models improve predictability of fluid performance in spacecraft systems where multiphase, particle-laden fluids may be used.

Earth Benefits: On Earth, particle-polymer suspensions underpin industries such as hydraulic fracturing, fiber spinning, extrusion molding, roll-to-roll manufacturing, and enhanced oil recovery. Adding particles imparts tailored mechanical or conductive properties but also increases energy demands due to altered rheology. This project provides mechanistic predictions for how particle orientation and polymer stress coupling influence flow resistance, helping optimize industrial processes, reduce energy consumption, and enable development of high-performance materials. By combining SHERE microgravity data with advanced modeling, this work addresses gaps in extensional rheology knowledge that hinder efficient design of complex fluid processing systems.

_source.Title: Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment
_source.Keywords: Polymers     Shearing     Complex flows     Elongation
_source.Objectives:
The objective of this investigation was to study the effect of pre-shear on the transient evolution of the microstructure and viscoelastic tensile stresses for monodisperse dilute polymer solutions. The SHERE flight experiment aimed to investigate and quantify, for the first time, the transient extensional stress growth characteristics of a dilute polymer solution after a defined pre-shear history.

Following the initial SHERE campaign a re-flight of the investigation was carried out as SHERE-R with additional experimental runs.
_source.Approach: The test fluid used for this investigation was a dilute solution (0.025 wt.%) of a narrow polydispersity high molecular weight polystyrene (Mw equals 2.25×106 g/mol, PDI ≈ 1.02) dissolved in oligomeric styrene oil. The FM core consists of two endplates and an inner shroud, which is slid back to deploy the fluid column between the two endplates. A steady shear rate between 0 and 50 s-1 is then imposed on the fluid sample by rotating one endplate from 0 to 500 rpm for a predetermined time (5 to 60 s) while holding the other endplate stationary. As soon as the rotation ceased, an elongational deformation was imposed by axially translating one of the endplates in an exponential manner in order to generate constant strain rates ranging from 0.1 to 5.0 s-1. The tensile force and filament shape were monitored during the stretching flow. The position of the moving plate is recorded to verify the imposed displacement profile. By backlighting the test fluid with an electroluminescent panel and viewing the fluid column from above with a video camera, one half of the (symmetric) fluid column shape was recorded for subsequent image analysis in order to determine the evolution in the filament profile during stretching and subsequent relaxation. The fluid and air temperatures were digitally recorded using thermistors for later post-processing and temperature correction. After cessation of the extensional flow, the experiment monitored the subsequent evolution of the midpoint radius (via a laser micrometer), the filament shape, and the tensile force in the column.
_source.Hypothesis: Constitutive equations for viscoelastic fluids such as dilute polymer solutions generally predict large changes in the extensional rheology of the material as the elongation rate is increased. This investigation attempts to test the validity of this hypothesis by performing experiment with dilute non-Newtonian polymer solutions in extensional flows.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates Earth-based processing operations. The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character. Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools. This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability. In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites. SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts. In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elastomer films, which are very resilient and can be made thin and lightweight. These elastomeric materials may form the basis of adhesives and fillers utilized in a wide variety of repair applications, especially under a reduced gravity environment, such as the repair of space suits or other similar materials. Understanding and exploiting the ability to fabricate new parts in-situ from a limited number of precursor components is critical in future space missions where weight plays a critical role in the overall cost of a mission. Additionally, in-situ repair provides a means of maintaining systems during transport and while on the Moon, Mars, and other extraterrestrial bodies.
Fundamental understanding and measurement of the extensional rheology of complex fluids also allows Earth-based manufacturing processes to be controlled and improved. Ground-based work using variants of the Filament Stretching Rheometer includes studies of spinnability, and the investigations of cohesive and adhesive instabilities which manifests themselves in adhesion and tackiness of materials. It has lead to the development of a Resin-spinning technology that allows the formation of ultra-fine elastic threads analogous to spider-silks. Control of the fluid shear history and extensional rheology of test fluid is essential to optimizing the ultimate web properties. Extensional rheology is of critical importance in optimization of polymer processing operations that involve complex flows, i.e. flows that contain both shearing (rotation) and elongation (stretching) components.

_source.Keywords: Colloids     microgravity     Crystals
_source.Objectives:
The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of ‘colloid engineering’, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors.  The BCAT-4 investigation had two primary objectives corresponding to specific samples:
Critical Point (BCAT-3-4-CP): Depending on their relative distances and energies with respect one another, atoms and molecules organize themselves to form gases, liquids, or solids. By varying the concentrations of the microscale spheres, this experiment studied the critical point of these systems where gases and liquids no longer exist as separate entities and a new state of matter forms when one reaches a critical point.
Polydispersion (BCAT-4-Poly): BCAT-4-Poly will use model hard-spheres (suspended in a liquid that makes them transparent) to explore pure and seeded colloidal crystal nucleation and the effects of polydispersity, providing insight into how to understand and control the processes used by nature to bring order out of disorder.
_source.Approach: BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintanence Work Area (MWA) on ISS.  The first set of samples was composed of mixtures of colloids and polymers near their liquid-gas critical point. The second set consisted of spherical colloidal particles with effective volume fractions resulting in an amorphous or glassy phase in normal gravity. The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells. The samples were manually homogenized using a stirbar (a teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette. Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.
_source.Hypothesis: Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth.  This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The findings of BCAT-4 can directly contribute to the development of advanced materials for use in space missions, such as lightweight and durable composites for spacecraft or self-assembling structures for space habitats. Additionally, understanding colloidal behavior aids in the optimization of life support systems, such as those used for water recycling and air purification, which are vital for sustaining long-duration missions to destinations like Mars. On Earth, the results of BCAT-4 have practical applications across multiple industries, including consumer goods, medicine, and manufacturing. For instance, the study of colloidal stability and crystallization informs the design of more stable food products, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical formulations. The findings also enhance industrial processes like 3D printing, where precise control of particle interactions is crucial for producing high-quality materials. Furthermore, BCAT-4 contributes to advancements in medicine by improving drug delivery systems that rely on colloidal suspensions, ensuring more effective treatments. By expanding the understanding of fundamental physical processes, BCAT-4 drives innovation in material design and production, benefiting diverse sectors and improving everyday products and technologies.

_source.Keywords: Colloids     Microgravity
_source.Objectives:
The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of colloid engineering, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors.  The BCAT-6 investigation had four primary objectives corresponding to specific samples:
Phase Separation (BCAT-6-Phase Seperation): to study how gas and liquid separate and join together in space. Colloidal liquids, which have tiny particles suspended throughout, are used to study how the two different phases interact. This research gives fundamental insight into the nature of supercritical fluids--fluids having both liquid and gas properties. This information could be used to develop colloidal materials that last longer.
Colloidal Disks (BCAT-6-Colloidal Disks): to improve understanding of properties of liquid crystals.
Polystyrene - Deoxyribonucleic Acid (BCAT-6-PS-DNA): to use DNA as a type of molecular glue to specifically stick small particles together. The experiment uses microscopic polymer beads in solution (colloids) that have been coated with DNA. The DNA only binds to its complement and hence keeps specific particles together to form designer crystals.
Seeded Growth (BCAT-6-Seeded Growth): to build on previous research looking at how dense groups of particles may be coaxed to form crystal structures when much larger “seed” particles are added. Some materials may consist of large individual crystals, or groups of many smaller crystals organized in a larger structure. Knowing when and how either type of crystal will form gives insight into how to control crystal growth which is important in many industrial processes.
_source.Approach: BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS.  The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in cuvettes in individual wells.  The samples were manually homogenized using a stir bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each cuvette.  Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using EarthKAM, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.
_source.Hypothesis: Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth. This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Colloidal phase separation research in microgravity supports both space and Earth applications, advancing technologies such as life-support systems, rocket fuels, and nanoparticle behavior in spacecraft. It enhances liquid crystals for astronaut helmets and energy-efficient displays while enabling space-based production of larger, higher-quality crystals. On Earth, studies of colloidal materials and liquid crystal models improve product shelf life, tunable displays, and molecular nanotechnology. Innovations include DNA-programmed crystals for advanced diagnostics, industrial materials, and next-generation electronics, benefiting industries like medicine, plastics, and consumer devices.

_source.Title: Pore-Mushy Zone Interaction during Directional Solidification of Alloys: Three Dimensional Simulation and Comparison with Experiments
_source.Keywords: Porosity     Dendritic Array     Phase Field     lattice Boltzmann     Mushy Zone     Simulation     cellular automaton
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI Grant
_source.Objectives:
The primary objective of this research was to develop a numerical 3D model capable of simulating the pore-mushy zone interaction during directional solidification of
Succinonitrile -Water alloys in microgravity and test the simulation results against the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) microstructural observations, quantitatively and qualitatively.
_source.Approach: This investigation exploited forefront methods in microscale solidification and developed models based on phase filed (PF), cellular automaton (CA) and Lattice Boltzmann (LB) to simulate pore formation and its motion during directional solidification. The results from the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) experiments were conducted in the microgravity environment aboard the Space Station with the intent of better understanding the role entrained porosity/bubbles play on microstructure during controlled directional solidification (DS). Several sets of time-temperature-interface-bubble interaction data were extracted and analyzed from the PFMI videos. The simulation results were tested against the PFMI microstructural observations.
_source.Hypothesis: Previous real time observations in transparent analogues of interactions between a bubble and an array of primary dendrites are essentially “two-dimensional” (2D) and are affected by the “wall” effects. Contrary to earlier belief, it is now recognized that the basic premise of such experiments, i.e. 2D dendrites represent morphology of a three-dimensional (3D) array, is false. This investigation hypothesizes that understanding pore-mushy zone interaction in real castings requires both the experimental observations and also the theoretical/numerical modeling with 3D array of dendrites.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This investigation helped to explain fundamental aspects of the mechanisms that regulate the formation of microporosities. The formation of these defects depends on microstructure features that cannot be properly captured by current meso- and macro-scale models based on averaging techniques. The direct numerical simulation of bubble dynamics in a dendritic network can provide a relation between macroscopically observable variables like cooling rate or temperature gradient and difficult to measure dynamic microscopic features like microporosity distribution, interdendritic permeability, solute redistribution, and dendrite arm spacing. This research not only provided valuable contribution to the understanding of pore-mushy zone interaction during solidification in the absence of gravity, which would be helpful for future in-space fabrication processes involving solidification, but it was a first step to quantitatively simulate such 3D interactions during terrestrial directional solidification in realistic size sample domains. Although much observation has been done in pictures of static microstructures at different stages of solidification, it has never been possible to capture the dynamic response of these features in an evolving mushy zone. This information is critical to assess, validate, and improve macroscale mushy zone models used in current casting and welding codes.

_source.Title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
_source.Keywords: DAFT     Condensate Nuclei Counter     Laser scattering aerosol device     Fire safety     Space hardware testing     P-Trak particulate counter     Capillary Fluid Motion     Combustion     Smoke     Fire prevention
_source.Objectives:
The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak,  to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
    1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
    2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
    3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
    4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
_source.Approach:
The experimental approach consists of the following components:

    1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
    2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
    3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
_source.Hypothesis:
The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates.

The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses:
    1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.
    2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity. This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts. Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

_source.Title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
_source.Keywords: SAFFIRE     Fire Safety     Surface Combustion     Smoldering     Flame Spread     low-gravity fire testing     flammability
_source.Objectives:
The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
_source.Approach: The Saffire-III experiments were performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire 1 investigation, the Saffire III investigation also used SIBAL as the sample material. However, the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I. The flow was either concurrent or opposed.  Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

_source.Title: Cool Flames Investigation
_source.Keywords: Droplet combustion     Extinction     Helium dilution     n-dodecane cool flames     Flame dynamics     Alkane chemistry     Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC)     Low-temperature chemistry     hydrocarbon fuel combustion     Renewable jet fuel
_source.Sponsoring Agency: ISSNL  National Laboratory - National Science Foundation (NL-NSF)
_source.Funding Source: ISSNL National Laboratory - National Science Foundation (NL-NSF)
_source.Objectives:
The objectives of this investigation are to:
    1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
    2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
    3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
    4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
_source.Approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.
_source.Hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

_source.Title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
_source.Keywords: Smoke     Surface Combustion     Fire Safety     Bio-Astronautics     Smoldering
_source.Objectives: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
_source.Approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated  spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
_source.Hypothesis:
The three hypotheses that motivated this investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.
