_source.Title: Packed Bed Reactor Experiment - Water Recovery
_source.Keywords: PBRE     Packed Bed Reactor Experiment     PBRE-WR
_source.Objectives: The objective of the flight experiment was to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different gas and liquid flow conditions. The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up. The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flow or flushes prior to beginning of the runs. Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates.
_source.Approach:
The PBRE-WR investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions. The approach can be summarized in the following key steps:

1. Ground-Based Research and Model Development:
Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds. This included:
   Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters.
   Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity.
   Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions.

2. Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment:
A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS. This involved:
   Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation.
   Selection of packing materials: PBRE-WR used 3.5 mm Alumina packing, a common inert material used in reactor beds such as water purification systems.
   Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios.

3. Execution of Spaceflight Experiments:
The PBRE-WR experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures. This involved:
   Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run.
   Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix.
   Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run.
   Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis.

4. Data Analysis and Interpretation:
The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to:
   Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings.
   Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models.
   Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes.
   Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop.

5. Dissemination of Results:
The findings of the PBRE-WR investigations have not been completed and disseminated yet.
_source.Hypothesis: While the overarching principles of two-phase flow in porous media apply, the specific material properties of alumina will cause unique flow phenomena, and models can be modified to account for such. Furthermore, this unique data is specifically relevant to the design and operation of reactors used in space-based water recovery systems, and the data can be used to improve and optimize such systems.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils. Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media. Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN). The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment- Microscopy
_source.Keywords: Polydispersity     Creams     Stabilization processes     Gels     Colloids
_source.Objectives: The ACE-M1 investigation aims to study the behavior of microscopic particles in colloidal mixtures such as gels and creams.  Objectives include the study of the physics of colloidal coarsening and the role of polydispersity (variation in particle size) in determining the stability of colloidal systems. Previous Earth-based experiments show that polydispersity dramatically affects the time it takes for these gels to collapse. The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
_source.Approach: The ACE-M1 investigation utilized a Sample Cartridge disk with 10 Sample Wells for 10 samples. Samples were colloidal fluids of small and large particles in varying concentration over .5 to 2.0 mg/ml.  Protocols included Homogenization and microscopic Observation and Imaging.  A crew member used  magnetic stir bars embedded in the sample well to homogenized each sample.  Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
_source.Hypothesis: Polydispersity significantly affects the time scale and dynamics of coarsening. It is believed that polydispersity can lead to a substantial difference in the collapse time of weak gels, and understanding this effect in a microgravity environment can provide critical insights into product design and stability.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Benefits: By conducting colloidal research in microgravity, the ACE-M1 experiment can obtain clearer data on the dynamics of liquid mixtures, free from the effects of gravitational forces. This research can improve the manufacturing processes for creating new, longer-lasting products for use both in space and on Earth.
Earth Benefits: Understanding the behavior of colloidal mixtures and the coarsening process can help materials scientists design products with longer shelf lives. This has significant implications for a wide range of products, including food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions, potentially leading to reduced waste and enhanced product performance​.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 7
_source.Keywords: Colloid     non-spherical     Self-assembly     depletant
_source.Objectives: The ACE-T7 experiment involves the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium. These so-called “self-assembled colloidal structures”, are vital to the design of advanced optical materials and active devices. The objective of  ACE-T7 was to utilize confocal microscopy for time- and space-resolved, 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids whose phases can be controlled by adding depletants and/or adjusting spatial temperature changes around a particular location. The research goal is to produce cubic colloidal structures, and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. ACE-T7 varied the size of the depletant in different samples with the goal of seeing the effect on crystallization.  The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
_source.Approach: The ACE-T7 experiment used the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) with enhancements. ACE-T7 utilized two sample cartridges, each having three temperature-controlled  capillaries for a total of six samples; each capillary volume has 50 mm length, 2.0 mm ID width, and 0.2 mm ID height, with automated mixing capabilities using magnetic stir bars embedded in the capillaries. Each sample volume was about 20 μl. Each cartridge could be heated or cooled uniformly via Peltier temperature control. The concentrations of hollow silica microcubes and silica nanoparticle depletants are varied to study the effect that each of these parameters have on the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth in microgravity. In total, six capillaries are prepared, numbered C1-C6. In capillaries C1-C4, the depletant concentration is kept constant at a concentration that produces cubic crystals in a timely manner on Earth (within 1 hour), while the concentration of hollow silica cubes is varied. In capillaries C5 and C6, the depletant concentration is increased and two different concentration of hollow silica cubes are used. After homogenization of each sample using the magnetic stirrer, the particles are left undisturbed to crystallize. Samples were preliminarily observed with a 2.5X objective, followed by measurements with 10X, 63X (air), 63X (oil), and 100X (oil) objectives.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that under certain conditions, the particles should self-organize into crystals with simple cubic symmetry, which is set by the size of the nano-size depletant. Increasing particle number density using a temperature gradient, i.e., thermophoresis, is expected to induce formation of crystallites. Three-dimensional structures that are impossible to create or reform on earth due to sedimentation issues (high density contrast between particles and fluid) should be observed in microgravity.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Future space exploration may use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves. Self-assembly and evolutionarily optimized functional units are key to long-duration space voyages which will require  use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves.  This research will enable design and development of functional colloidal structures for new devices for chemical energy, communication, and photonics, including photonic materials to control and manipulate light. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry. The beginning of this process is understanding the basic interactions between micro- and nanoscale particles, and how to control them using external sources such as temperature and light.

_source.Title: Advanced Structurally Embedded Thermal Spreader II Oscillating Head Pipes
_source.Keywords: Air Force     Oscillating heat pipes     OHP     Heat Pipes
_source.Objectives: The three primary science objectives are to measure the initial on-orbit thermal performance, to measure long duration thermal performance, and to assess any lifetime degradation. Flight data will be used to validate microgravity portions of an OHP operating limits model recently published by members of the team. Returned flight experiment hardware will be subjected to post-flight testing to assess the presence of any non-condensable gas that may have formed on orbit.
_source.Approach: The ASETS-II experiment is made of three low-mass, low-cost OHPs and an electronics experiment control box. The three OHPs are of varying configuration (center heating with single- and double-sided cooling) and working fluids (butane and R-134a) in order to isolate specific performance parameters of interest. In addition to serving as a science experiment, the ASETS-II flight experiment serves as a pathfinder for incorporating high performance OHP-based thermal spreaders into flat plate structures such as electronics chip carriers, thermal ground planes, and spacecraft panels. Microgravity influence on fluid flow, especially two-phase flow, is significantly different than in a terrestrial environment. This is true for steady-state operations, but is more important for transient operation. In addition, the combined effects of the space environment (e.g. thermal Cutaway of an oscillating heat pipe (OHP) showing its microchannel pattern cycling, high vacuum, charging, vibration) are required to verify the performance of the system on orbit for long durations.
_source.Hypothesis: Oscillating heat pipes will exhibit consistent and stable thermal performance in a long-duration microgravity environment, comparable to their performance in a terrestrial setting.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Potentially shift the way NASA designs its future deep space craft and extraterrestrial human habitats, providing safer, more reliable temperature regulation for the human occupants and the sensitive technology housed inside Cooling electronics.

_source.Title: Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-3
_source.Keywords: Colloids     magnetorheological (MR) fluids     self-assembly     microgravity     pulsed fields
_source.Objectives: InSPACE-3 investigated the assembly of paramagnetic colloidal ellipsoids in pulsed magnetic fields.  An objective was to study the effect of particle shape on the kinetics of aggregation and structures formed by DC and pulsed magnetic fields in suspensions of superparamagnetic particles. Specifically, the investigation studied the suspensions of paramagnetic ellipsoid-shaped particles and quantify the effect of particle shape on the interactions of dipolar chains and the  resulting suspension microstructure.
_source.Approach: InSPACE-3 employed video microscopy to obtain suspension structural information. Two particle shapes were tested for four frequency conditions and four field strengths, for a total of 24 experimental runs. Each run took approximately one hour. Each sample had a particle volume fraction of 0.52%. This concentration represents an optimum value based on previous microgravity experiments, designed to balance the ability to capture aggregation kinetics at short times in DC fields the structural evolution in pulsed fields such that the final coalescence stage is observed. For detailed experimental approach please refer Science Requirements Document (SRD).
_source.Hypothesis: Based on the science results of InSPACE-2,  InSPACE-3 hypothesizes that particle shape will alter the aggregation kinetics, microstructures and microscopic mechanics, such as buckling instabilities that are observed for suspensions of polarizable spheres. This research will potentially lead to the ability to engineer enhanced properties of these suspensions, including the ability to suppress lateral aggregation in magnetorheological fluid-based electromechanical devices or the ability to create new functional materials that control the flow of electromagnetic and thermal energy.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The quick phase-shifting property of magnetic colloidal fluids studied in InSPACE-3 makes them potentially useful for devices such as optical interfaces, active noise, and vibration dampers inside spacecrafts.  Future uses could include robotics, energy-transfer devices such as clutches, and other control systems and on Earth directed self-assembly of crystalline structures from particles that may eventually allow creation of new nano-materials fabricated from nanoparticle building blocks, with potential applications in medicine, energy storage, chemical separations, and catalysis. Magnetic colloidal fluid technology is currently used for shock absorbers in race cars and sport cars.  This technology is expanding to include making large-scale building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

_source.Title: Cold Atom Lab - Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space
_source.Keywords: Ultracold Atoms     Atomic Clocks     Atom Interferometry     Microgravity Environments     Quantum Sensors
_source.Objectives:
The Consortium’s work is described in the context of four Tasks.
  Task 1: Advanced Clocks in Space and Time Transfer
  Task 2: Maturing and Advancing Atom Interferometer Technology for Space
  Task 3: Precision Atom Interferometric Measurement in Space
  Task 4: Strategies for the Frontier of Ultracold Atoms in Space.


The Consortium is: N. P. Bigelow, M. Kasevick, W. Ketterle, M. Lukin, H. Müller, W. D. Phillips, D. Pritchard, D. Stamper-Kurn, V. Vuletic, and J. Ye.
Berkeley and Stanford lead Tasks 2 and 3. MIT, U.C./JILA, and Harvard lead Task 1. U. Md., Rochester, and MIT lead Task 4.
Members of the Consortium can and often will contribute to all four tasks with priorities being set by the lead institutions.
_source.Approach:
The Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space (CUAS), led by Nicholas Bigelow, conducted groundbreaking experiments in atomic clocks, atom interferometry, and quantum gases, with a strong focus on the application of these quantum technologies in space environments. The consortium's research was guided by the objectives outlined in the National Research Council (NRC) report and NASA's Research Announcement (NRA), particularly in precision measurement and quantum gas studies. The Consortium fostered a collaborative approach, bringing together scientists from top institutions like MIT, Stanford, Berkeley, and Harvard, as well as international partners such as those from the DLR (German Space Agency). This collaboration allowed the group to pool expertise, regularly refine their goals, and push forward only the most promising space experiments.

The procedure for the creation of an ultracold gas is fairly standardized. The atoms are released into a vacuum chamber, collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), and cooled via laser cooling. The sample is then optically pumped to a low magnetic field seeking quantum state and transfer from the MOT to an atom-chip based trap. The atoms are then evaporatively cooled to below the critical temperature so that a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) begins to form. The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, and eventually the atoms are completely released from the trap and allowed to expand freely. At this point, the ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. After a prespecified time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC because the measurement process destroys the sample. A total of two images are taken, the first being an image of the sample and the second being a reference image that is taken after the destructive absorption imaging process.  This general process was followed by the Consortium for experiments requiring the production or probing of ultracold quantum gases.

In their work on atom interferometry, the Consortium conducted experiments to detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. The team also focused on measuring the fine structure constant with high accuracy, which involved overcoming systematic effects that could be amplified in the space environment. Collaborations with the Bose-Einstein Condensate and Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other international partners were essential for demonstrating long coherence times in microgravity, testing the equivalence principle, and searching for dark-energy candidates. These experiments were conducted with a focus on utilizing the microgravity conditions available aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and other space-based platforms, which provided a unique environment to achieve results unattainable on Earth.

In the realm of atomic clocks and quantum sensors, the Consortium developed new configurations for optical lattice clocks and achieved precision at the 19th decimal place, setting a new record for stable laser performance with a linewidth of 10 mHz. These experiments were designed to improve the accuracy of space-based timekeeping and navigation systems, which are critical for the success of space missions. The Consortium also explored innovative cooling methods, such as direct optical cooling to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation, which simplified the setup for quantum experiments in space. These methods were tested and refined in microgravity environments, demonstrating their potential to enhance the performance of quantum technologies in space.

Overall, the Consortium’s approach to conducting experiments was characterized by a strong emphasis on leveraging the unique conditions of space, particularly microgravity, to achieve results that would be impossible on Earth. Their collaborative efforts, cutting-edge experimental designs, and focus on precision allowed them to make significant contributions to the field of quantum technologies in space, laying the groundwork for future space missions and advancing our understanding of fundamental physics.
_source.Hypothesis: This consortium aims to provide a space for the world’s experts on Bose-Einstein Condensates (BEC), atom optics, atom interferometry, and related quantum realms to push the current boundaries of quantum gas and atomic physics space experiments. It is hypothesized that with the realization of a space atom laser and precision atomic interferometry there is potential for significant scientific advancement by testing the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model. A space atom laser is expected to provide truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter. Varied experiments and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control are hypothesized to mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind opportunity to investigate interacting quantum gases in space.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Significant progress has been made on atomic interferometry and atomic clocks in terrestrial experiments. The work has long-term impact for fundamental science, navigation technologies, and global clock synchronization. Clocks are vital to navigation, communication, and security.

ATOM INTERFEROMETRY
We have pushed atom interferometry for space applications forward in many ways:
  1. We have shown that atom interferometry can detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity. There is a chance to cover all the relevant parameter space so as to detect them or to rule them out once and for all. This work has been published in Science, Nature Physics, and Physical Review D.
  2. We have demonstrated a theoretically predicted, but never observed, attractive force on atoms from blackbody radiation. It is an important limitation that has to be taken into account in the design of atomic-physics space missions.
  3. We have pushed forward the accuracy of atom interferometry for measuring the fine structure constant, which has resulted in a measurement of this constant with an accuracy about three times better than the best previous one. The agreement of this measurement with others sets very strong constraints on hypothesized particles from the dark sector, such as dark photons.
  4. We have developed atom interferometry with lithium atoms, opening up the possibility to do interferometry with a much wider class of atoms than available previously. We will continue to develop atom interferometry for demonstrating the gravitational Aharonov-Bohm effect, and measuring fundamental constants very precisely. We will also work with the Bose-Einstein Condensate Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other teams to identify future targets for spaceborne fundamental physics. The interferometry work has several main thrusts. In the first thrust, we have been investigating how spaceborne atom interferometry can probe models for dark matter and dark energy. This has resulted in experimental demonstrations of such tests for so-called chameleon and symmetron models, and theoretical studies on how to make detailed predictions of the putative signals. In the second thrust, we have developed strategies to overcome systematic effects in atom interferometers that use Bragg diffraction, as the one planned for the Cold Atom lab. In the third, we have developed specific plans for spaceborne atom interferometry. We have collaborated with the German team Document for atom interferometry on the Cold Atom Lab and BECCAL. Plans include demonstrating long coherence times thanks to microgravity, tests of the equivalence principle, and searches for dark-energy candidates. They have also collaborated with Nan Yu (Jet Propulsion Laboratory-JPL) on a concept study QTEST (Quantum test of the Equivalence Principle and Spacer-Time) for testing the equivalence principle in space.

CLOCKS AND QUANTUM SENSORS TECHNOLOGIES
We have demonstrated the first direct optical cooling to Bose-Einstein condensation, without any evaporative cooling. This has promising impact of simplifying spaceborne experiments. The Bose-Einstein condensation by direct optical cooling was achieved for small ensembles of ~1000 atom. We will attempt to make substantially larger condensates with the same method by using a more powerful trapping laser. We have been working on spin squeezing in the optical-transition clock with trapped ytterbium atoms. By implementing both frequency and intensity feedback loops for the magical wavelength trap inside an optical cavity, we have now lengthened the trap lifetime for the Yb sample from 200 ms to 2 seconds. We have also started non-destructive state-dependent measurements for spin squeezing by observing the light transmitted through the cavity, and we can already more than resolve the shot-noise limit. In the Rb experiment, we are working towards using Rydberg states for increasing the light-atom interaction in cavity QED. We have frequency-stabilized the control laser coupling the P state to high-lying Rydberg states. We have demonstrated a new optical lattice clock configuration using a three-dimensional optical lattice, leading to measurement precision in the 19th decimal place. We have also demonstrated another record-breaking performance on stable lasers, with the narrowest laser linewidth at 10 mHz. We will perform a clock comparison between this JILA Sr clock and the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Yb clock and Search for ultralight dark matter by comparing the Sr transition frequency with the resonance frequency of a crystalline cavity.2022 Update: Our team aims to study: o The realization of a space atom laser o Precision atom interferometry in space o The investigation and manipulation of quantum gas sample control including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control
Relevance: Potential for significant scientific advancement from interferometric tests of the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model. Space atom laser provides truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter. Varied experiments of the investigation and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind investigations for interacting quantum gases in space.

_source.Title: Cold Atom Lab - Development of Atom Interferometry Experiments for the ISS
_source.Keywords: Atom Interferometry     Precision Quantum Metrology     Precision Inertial Sensing
_source.Objectives: Development of Atom Interferometry Experiments for the International Space Station's Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL- Atom Interferometry) demonstrates using atom interferometry as a precision measurement technique on the space station. Atom interferometry is an ultra-sensitive measurement technique that splits the quantum wave function of an atom into two distinct wave packets that travel separate trajectories and then recombine. This technique, already demonstrated on the ground, should work better in space and could be useful for future space navigation systems.
_source.Approach:
This investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The approach for the flight-based investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized.
1.	Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas:
•	Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned.
•	State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region.
•	Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures.
•	Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases.
2.	Manipulation and Probing:
•	Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements.
•	Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample.

This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. This investigation utilizes the atom interferometry equipment aboard the CAL instrument for precision measurement experiments. The BEC formed according to the steps laid out in the Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gases section is split using an off resonance standing wave laser. The split waves packets will travel different trajectories, and then recombine after a secondary laser beam is applied. After the recombination, the atomic interference pattern can be collected. The flight-based results can be compared to theoretical investigations and ground studies done at JPL, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that, combined with the current atomic cooling techniques, the implementation of expansion cooling will produce atoms with temperatures on the order of a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero (10^-12 K). With the unique settings provided by Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) the maximum expansion and low temperature limits are able to be probed. Atomic interferometry can be used to measure the acceleration of cold atoms relative to the International Space Station, allowing investigators to explore using ultracold atoms as part of an inertial navigation system.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The development of precision inertial sensing techniques is useful for Earth-based as well as space-based navigation. Besides using direct sensing for inertial navigation, rotation sensing can also be useful for north-finding while gravity sensing can be used to tabulate local gravity variations and form a type of three-dimensional map for navigating.

These techniques also have many applications in geophysics. Gravity sensing can be used for oil and mineral exploration, while rotation sensing can detect dynamics in the Earth's core. Gravity sensing also has defense applications such as locating underground tunnels and potential screening cargo for high-density contraband or weapons.

Other precision measurement applications have less direct impact, but advance scientific knowledge. For instance, precision tune-out spectroscopy measurements of atomic matrix elements can be used to improve the interpretation of atomic parity violation experiments. These in turn impact our understanding of the standard model of particle physics and thus the nature of our universe. Direct benefits of such understanding can be hard to trace, but in general the continued advance of technological applications builds on advances in our fundamental knowledge.

_source.Title: Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures-2 Reflight
_source.Keywords: Ostwald Ripening     Microgravity     Coarsening     Kinetics
_source.Objectives: The objective of the CSLM-2R investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the focus on lower solid volume percent  samples.
_source.Approach: The CSLM-2R approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM-2 investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2R were 0.05. 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 and the coarsening times ranged from 1.6 to 48 hours.
_source.Hypothesis: The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

_source.Title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
_source.Keywords: chemical kinetics     ethane     heat loss     low-temperature combustion     porous burner     dilution     formaldehyde     intensified video camera     n-butane     negative-temperature coefficient
_source.Proposal Title: ISS: Collaborative Research: Spherical Cool Diffusion Flames Burning Gaseous Fuels
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Science Foundation (NSF)  Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS)
_source.Objectives:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
_source.Approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
_source.Hypothesis:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

_source.Title: Cold Atom Lab - Zero-G Studies of Few Body and Many-Body Physics
_source.Keywords: Few Body Physics     Quantum Mechanics     Quantum Gases     Exotic States of Matter     Efimov Physics
_source.Objectives: Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions. The dynamics of few-body systems comprised of just three or four atoms can strongly influence the collective behavior of quantum gases and play an important role in development of quantum gas applications. Modern laser cooling techniques are used to chill atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions. The acquired data fills a critical need for the development of detailed and precise atomic physics models. The development of these models is performed in theoretical studies accompanying the data gathering campaigns with the CAL instrument. Studying the behavior and interaction of few atoms in microgravity could provide important data for developing a precise theory describing quantum gases on a microscopic level. The knowledge gained in this study also aids in the development of future quantum technologies for which a detailed microscopic understanding of few-body physics is essential. Examples of future quantum technologies include, among others, atom interferometers for inertial navigation or precision measurements of gravity and sensitive Terahertz (THz) detectors for astronomy.
_source.Approach:
The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study few-body physics and exotic quantum states. Modern laser-cooling techniques are used to cool atoms to near absolute zero temperatures. At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics. Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions.

1. Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas:
    • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique is based on the rapid scattering of light off atoms and can cool a cloud of atoms to temperatures below 1x10-3 K. An additional magnetic field applied in conjunction with the lasers concentrates the cold atoms in a specific region of the vacuum apparatus, called the source chamber. The MOT is the starting point for further cooling and experimental preparation.
    • State Preparation: Using further laser manipulations, the atoms are then prepared in a state that seeks to occupy regions of low magnetic fields. By applying a suitable magnetic field geometry with a moving magnetic minimum, the cloud of atoms is transported to a so-called “science region.” Magnetic fields generated by a chip with current-carrying traces provide a trap for the atoms in the science region.
    • Evaporative Cooling: With the atoms trapped in the science region, evaporative cooling is performed by selectively removing the hottest rubidium atoms from the cloud. The remaining atoms then rethermalize at a lower temperature. The selective removal of the hottest rubidium atoms is achieved by applying suitably tuned radiofrequency radiation. Potassium atoms are cooled by being in thermal contact with the actively cooled rubidium atoms, in a process called sympathetic cooling, where rubidium atoms act as a cold bath of atoms. With sufficient evaporative cooling, the clouds of rubidium and potassium atoms can undergo a phase transition to a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), providing a macroscopic, quantum mechanical object. However, pronounced quantum mechanical effects can already be observed before reaching this phase transition.
    • Further sample preparation: After the preparation of the ultracold sample, further preparation steps are employed for the proposed studies. These steps include changes to the trapping strength, changes of the internal states of the atoms, and the application of suitable homogeneous magnetic fields.

2. Manipulation and Detection:
    • Manipulation Techniques: The ultracold gas is manipulated using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. In addition, homogeneous magnetic fields are used to shift internal energy levels of the atoms.  These techniques are designed to adjust the pairwise interactions as needed for the preparation of exotic quantum states.
    • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time-of-flight during which the cloud is released from the trap and can expand freely, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. For this, a short laser pulse is flashed onto the atoms, and the shadow cast by the atoms is imaged on a CCD camera using a custom microscope setup. This imaging process typically destroys the “quantumness” of the sample and concludes an experimental cycle. The apparatus then starts over with the preparation of a new sample. Many cycles are performed during a typical data-taking campaign, with a time scale of approximately one minute per run.
_source.Hypothesis: Ultracold atoms in microgravity provide a unique environment for the study of complex few-body phenomena. One of the surprising predictions for quantum mechanical few-body systems is the existence of universality, i.e. the idea that highly intricate phenomena can be governed by underlying principles that are agnostic to specific microscopic realizations. As a concrete example, Efimov physics predicts the emergence of an infinite series of exotic three-body bound states when the interactions between the atoms are made stronger and stronger. It is predicted that these Efimov states are connected by universal scaling relations governing their energy and their size. Our experiments aim to provide essential benchmark data to test this universality hypothesis. By measuring two members of this infinite series, scaling relations can be probed and can be compared to some of the most advanced few-body theories to date. This will be a steppingstone towards the investigation of a plethora of associated few-body phenomena, with the ultimate goal of significantly advancing the boundary of our understanding and paving the way for the development of new quantum technologies.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Physics is the discipline that provides understanding of biology and chemistry at the most microscopic level, and the area within physics most relevant to chemistry and biology is “few-body physics.” It is an often neglected portion of physics, because it is so difficult to do. An important way to make progress is to simplify, simplify, simplify: to come up with model systems in which we can make progress that can later be applied to human-centric disciplines like biology, and develop exotic and useful new materials. A promising way to simplify is to study matter at lower temperature, and lower densities. The Cold-Atom Lab (CAL) flying in the International Space Station (ISS) is where we will reach the lowest possible temperatures, and low densities, to perform studies of simple, yet intricate (think “snowflakes”) clusters of three or four atoms.

Ultracold atomic gases are a key platform for a broad range of future quantum technologies, including ultraprecise sensing and timekeeping, novel medical imaging methods, secure communication schemes, high-performance computing, and development of exotic materials. A precise knowledge of few-body physics is necessary to fully realize the potential of quantum technologies. This project supports development of a detailed understanding of quantum mechanical few-body physics at the microscopic level, which may open new avenues for quantum gas applications in future space exploration. Such applications include inertial navigation and precision measurements using atom interferometry, or calibration standards for detectors used in astronomy.

_source.Title: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-2
_source.Keywords: STDCE-1     STDCE-2     Constant Flux     Surface Tension     Thermocapillary Flow     USML-2
_source.Objectives:
The main objectives of the present work are to investigate:
   1. The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows.
   2. The effect of the heating mode and the static free surface shape on the oscillations.
   3. The shape and motion of the free surface during oscillations.
   4. The coupling among the free surface deformation, the surface temperature distribution, and the velocity field.
_source.Approach:
The STDCE-2 investigation employed a systematic approach to explain the role of free surface deformation in oscillatory thermocapillary flows under microgravity conditions. This approach comprised:

Controlled Variation of Key Parameters:
   -Container Size: Utilizing three chamber diameters (1.2 cm, 2.0 cm, 3.0 cm) allowed researchers to examine the influence of scale on the onset of oscillations and assess potential inertial effects.
   -Heating Mode: Employing both submerged heater (CT mode) and CO2 laser (CF mode) systems enabled the comparison of flow behavior under constant temperature difference and constant heat flux boundary conditions, respectively.
   -Free Surface Shape: Tests were conducted with flat, concave, and convex free surfaces to explore the interplay between surface curvature and flow dynamics.

 Advanced Diagnostic Techniques:
   -Flow Visualization: The use of tracer particles enabled the visualization and qualitative characterization of flow patterns, including the three-dimensional, time-dependent structures observed during oscillations.
   -Infrared Imaging: An infrared scanner captured the temperature distribution across the oil's free surface, providing insights into the thermal gradients driving the thermocapillary flow and their evolution during oscillations.
   -Optical Deformation Measurement: A Ronchi system was employed to measure the free surface deformation and motions, allowing researchers to quantify the dynamic changes in surface shape and correlate them with observed flow behavior and temperature variations.

Interactive Operation:
The experiment was conducted interactively, allowing the researchers on the ground to communicate with the astronauts onboard the Spacelab, observe the downlinked video images in real-time, and adjust test parameters based on the observed phenomena. This flexibility facilitated the exploration of unexpected results and the fine-tuning of the experimental conditions to optimize data collection. The STDCE-2 investigation gathered comprehensive data aimed at complex dynamics of oscillatory thermocapillary flows and verifying the hypothesized role of free surface deformation in their onset.
_source.Hypothesis:
The onset of oscillatory thermocapillary flow, particularly in microgravity environments, is significantly influenced by free surface deformation, which acts in conjunction with the Marangoni number (Ma).
•	Buoyancy masks the true oscillation mechanism in Earth- based experiments: The experimental data on oscillatory thermocapillary flows taken in normal gravity environments are
        often confusing or contradictory due to the presence of buoyancy. This suggests that buoyancy may obscure the role of free surface deformation in the oscillation process.
•	Marangoni number alone is insufficient to predict oscillations in microgravity: The unexpected stability observed in the prior STDCE microgravity experiments, even at Marangoni
        numbers exceeding the critical threshold observed in ground-based tests, indicates that Ma is not the sole determinant of oscillatory onset in the absence of buoyancy.
•	Free surface deformation is a key factor: The interaction between thermocapillary forces and free surface deformation plays a key role in the oscillation mechanism.

Person.Last Name: Yuan Fortenberry Urban Yang Cleary Mulholland
Person.First Name: Zeng-guang Claire David Jiann Thomas George

_source.Keywords: Soot     Flames     Pyrell     SAME     Transmission Electron Microscopy     Silicon Rubber     Spacecraft Fire Safety     Teflon     Cotton     Smoke     Kapton     SAME-2
_source.Objectives: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.
_source.Approach:
SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material,
Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.
_source.Hypothesis:
The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation:
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories. Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

_source.Title: Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation
_source.Keywords: Directional Solidification     thermocapillary convection     International Space Station     pore formation     microgravity     succinonitrile analogue
_source.Proposal Title: Towards Understanding Pore Formation and Mobility During Controlled Directional Solidification
_source.Objectives: The scientific objective of the investigation was to observe porosity formation and its movement. Methods to minimize porosity and its influence will also be examined. Experimental variables that was investigated include, but are not limited to, bubble size, bubble number, imposed temperature gradient, material properties, and the effect of applying vibration to the system. The role of ''spring and piston'' assemblages and in-situ thermocouples was also investigated and assessed.
_source.Approach: The experimental approach consisted of employing a 10mm inside diameter quartz tubes on the order of 30 cm in length that was filled with pure succinonitrile (SCN) and SCN to which a small amount of water has been added to simulate alloy solidification. To investigate pore formation the sample tubes was filled by, at least, the three following methods. (1) Pieces of SCN was put in the tube. (2) SCN was cast into the tube. (3) SCN was cast into the tube and then be directionally solidified. Case 1 ensured porosity in the sample, case 2 allowed porosity to develop, and case 3 was prepared with the intent of minimizing porosity. Each sample tube was outfitted with an effective “spring and piston” assemblage and in-situ thermocouples. While thermocouples were required to accurately characterize the temperatures and temperature gradients they could also act as sites for pore nucleation and holding. The sample tubes were then inserted in a directional solidification furnace, which establishes a temperature gradient in the liquid and permits observation of the molten region. The furnace mounts on g-limit, a MSFC developed vibration isolation platform; this assemblage fits and was designed to operate within the ISS microgravity Glovebox. Porosity, which forms in the samples, was tracked and recorded with two video cameras set at 90 degrees from each other and orthogonal to the sample tube.
_source.Hypothesis: Direct observation of pore/bubble formation and their mobility during processing in a microgravity environment will provide insight regarding the minimization of this detrimental feature during solidification processing of important metal alloys and semiconductors.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: PFMI provides insight on how materials solidify in the space environment. Once this process is understood and improvements are made, future manufacturing processes can take place in the microgravity environment providing robust products. On Earth, materials that contain pores created and trapped during solidification degrade properties and cause a distinct weakening in the overall structure of the cast product. Examples of these materials include semiconductors and aircraft turbine blades.

Person.Last Name: Liggieri Ferri Misono Orsi Antoni Clausse Yamashita Sakamoto Ravera Miller Fischer Noskov Hashimoto Rubio Schneck Ouazzani Karapantsios Rossetti Elliott Cassi Loglio Cristofolini Starov Dutschk Makievski

_source.Keywords: Foams     Soft Matter Dynamics
_source.Objectives:
The work proposed in the PASTA project follows the line from characterizing the surface properties of particles via a complex analysis of the properties of layers at liquid/gas and liquid/liquid interfaces to studying the behaviour of liquid films and finally to model real foams and emulsions. The work comprises the application of available knowledge to the preparation and characterization of particle stabilized emulsions, produced by adapting to the Soft Matter Dynamics instrument.

The role of gravity on quiescent wet foams can be captured in 2 key questions:

Is the growth law for average bubble size R~√ time, such that R dR/dt is a constant? If so, what is the liquid-fraction dependence of this rate?
How do the rate and the nature of the bubble rearrangement dynamics change as the liquid fraction is increased to the point of un-jamming (transition solid-like to liquid-like)?
PASTA will address the SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES:

Evaluate the characteristic time for the droplet coalescence as a function of the formulation
Identify and investigate specific dynamic regimes for droplets dynamics (for example Brownian vs. Capillarydriven) during emulsion destabilization.
Test and develop models for emulsion stability/destabilization prognosis.
_source.Approach:
The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS.
Each PASTA sample cell is fitted with a piston that allows to agitate the mixture within the cell at various frequencies and durations to emulsify the mixture. The sample cells are grouped 4-by-4 in sample cell units that can be fitted on a carousel inside SMD. This carousel allows for placing each individual sample cell in the diagnostics position of SMD, where it can be observed with the SMD sensors and several diagnostic tools, like the overview camera that takes microscope image sequences in black and white of the sample cell.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods. Both stable and unstable emulsions are needs that are shared across a variety of applications. For example, efficient de-emulsifiers are needed to facilitate the process of phase separation (breaking) in the crude oil emulsions extracted from the wells, while high stability oil-in-water emulsions are required in the final stage of production of the same well or to facilitate pumping high-viscosity oils through pipelines. In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability. However, destabilizing emulsions are key to processing raw food materials such as milk and vegetable oils.

_source.Title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II

Person.First Name: Paul Carlos Fletcher J. James Subrata

_source.Keywords: Flame Spread     extinction limits     MSG     Fire Suppression     Solid Fuels     Forced Flow Velocity     BASS     Fire Safety
_source.Objectives:
BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
  1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
  2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
  3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements.
  4)  Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.

The primary variables include:
     • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction)
     • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation)
     • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets
_source.Approach: To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.
_source.Hypothesis:
BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2
concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

_source.Title: Physics of Hard Spheres Experiment
_source.Keywords: Colloids     Order-disorder transition     Bragg's Light Scattering     Microgravity     Hard sphere     Nucleation and growth     Non-linear rheology
_source.Objectives: By significantly reducing gravitational sedimentation the primary objective of this microgravity investigation was to quantify the volume fractions at which dispersions of hard spheres freeze, melt, and become glasses; the equilibrium structure associated with each phase; the dynamics of Brownian fluctuations in each phase; the kinetics of the nucleation and growth of the crystalline phase; the static elastic modulus of the crystalline and glassy phases; the low shear viscosity from the freezing point to close packing, and the yield stress and plasticity of the crystalline phase.
_source.Approach: The experiment involved making a series of measurements on approximately 8 different samples of different concentrations (i.e. volume fractions of PMMA in an index matching fluid).  The samples were made from a mixture of decalin, tetralin, and PMMA spheres with a stabilizing polymer grafted onto them.  The decalin (index - 1.48) and the tetralin (index - 1.54) was mixed in a combination which index matches the PMMA (index - 1.51), allowing the use of single photon counting techniques to probe the particle dynamics at different concentrations.  Once in orbit, the experiment was initialized and each of the samples melted to start the nucleation and growth phase.  After melting, each sample was examined to ensure that complete melting has occurred, and immediate static scattering measurements will begin and progress for 24 hours on the nucleating sample. After each melting phase, a concentration dependent nucleation and growth phase occurred and was monitored by static light scattering measurements.  These measurements proceeded while the experiment entered into an equilibration phase during which longer range order formed. The static light scattering measurements proceeded until the Bragg peaks were well developed and sufficient data for ensemble averages were taken for a sound statistical basis for the conclusions intended to experimentally ascertain.  Periodic measurements, both static and dynamic, were made to gage the progress and determine if alternate procedures are required. During this period, dynamic light scattering measurements were performed on the nucleating sample.  Other measurements such as rheology measurements were performed on the other seven samples after this 24 hours period.
_source.Hypothesis: Some colloids (a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid) have the ability to act like a gas, liquid, solid, or even glass, depending on the relative concentration between the suspended material and the solution they are suspended in, and/or the presence or absence of gravity. The behavior of a densely packed colloid here on earth mimics glass in the distribution of its particles, while in space, the same density colloid acts more closely like a solid. This results in a highly organized, lattice-like arrangement of particles in the colloid. It is hypothesized that the complete set of data from the microgravity experiments to test scalings proposed in the literature, e.g. the shear rate dependence of the viscosity and the rate of crystal growth with either the short- or the long-term self diffusion coefficient; the relationships among the osmotic pressure, the static shear modulus, and the yield stress for solid phases.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The colloidal engineering process will play a fundamental role in the creation of new materials and products in space, such as optical switches and lasers for communications and displays, and 3D Bragg crystals for controlling light. Understanding the physics describing the Packing of Hard Spheres has everyday impacts and benefits here on earth including Grain packing; Structure of Liquids, Solids and Glasses; Freezing Transition; Flow and Plasticity of Sand; Optimization of data storage and transmission in the presence of Noise and Opto-electronic Materials, Light Localization and Photonic Bandgaps. The ultimate payoff will be a definitive set of data for the hard spheres useful for (a) testing fundamental correlations among physical properties, (b) serving as a reference for understanding the behavior of systems with more complex interaction potentials, and (c) guiding attempts to control or modify the structure of densely packed media.

_source.Title: Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 2
_source.Keywords: capillary channels     Capillary Flow     CCF
_source.Objectives: The investigation aims to determine critical flow rates (choking) for wedge channels across various lengths and wedge angles. It explores choking behavior across capillary-inertial, visco-capillary, and overlap flow regimes. Bubble transport, migration, and phase separation within wedge geometries will also be investigated, focusing on the influence of flow rate, channel length, and bubble diameter.
_source.Approach: The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG. The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry. Initially, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned. Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed. The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop. The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module. The fluid management technology built into the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.
_source.Hypothesis: The central hypothesis for CCF-CV EU2 is that a critical flow rate limit also exists in open capillary channels with wedge and gapped-wedge geometries, and it is governed by the interplay of capillary, viscous, and inertial forces. It is expected that the critical flow rate will be a function of the channel geometry, which includes the wedge angle and channel length, and that there will be different flow regimes which are linked to the governing flow forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the nature of bubble transport, migration, and phase separation will depend on the flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length, as well as bubble properties, such as the size and frequency.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces. The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices.
The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration. The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions. The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts. Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales. This can be encountered when a wetting liquid wicks into a porous structure. It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect. In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic. The main difference is that the flow was not driven by the capillary forces. Instead, the capillary forces were used to stabilize the flow path. A variety of applications on Earth may have this requirement as well.

_source.Keywords: Foams     Diffuse Transmission Spectroscopy     Bubble Dynamics     Coarsening
_source.Objectives: The objective is to take advantage of microgravity to eliminate drainage and to use imaging and multiple light scattering diagnostics in order to non-invasively measure and elucidate the time evolution of key features of the bubble-packing structure of wet foams – namely, the bubble size distribution and bubble rearrangement dynamics – and how they are affected by degree of wetness by systematically increasing the liquid content for sequences of otherwise identical foams. FOAM is divided into two experiments: FOAM Coarsening and FOAM Stability.
_source.Approach:
Experiment Cells
The FOAM-C experimental set-up comprises five segments with a total of 20 small test cells containing a variety of liquid mixtures. The Fluid Science Laboratory on the ISS Columbus module will automatically shake and analyze these mixtures using complex laser optics, highly sensitive photodiodes and high-resolution cameras that can take up to 10,000 images per second.

Each test cell weighs only 20 grams and contains less than 2 cm³ of the liquid mixture, while each segment comprises four test cells and weighs a total of 320 grams.

Diagnostics
- Overview video,
- Multiple light scattering spectroscopies (SVS - Speckle Variance Spectroscopy and/or DWS - Diffusing-Wave Spectroscopy)

Example of Protocols
- First, the foam is made at the time T0. Then the foam is left to age while optical diagnostics measure its dynamics during aging (up to 24 hours foam age). These cycles can be repeated several times. Another cell with a different composition (liquid fraction, concentration) is then subject of a new series of experiments.
- Granular matter samples of defined volume concentration shall be agitated until a steady state is reached.
Consequently, optical diagnostics measure the grains dynamics in the steady state and after turning the agitation off.

Experiment Protocol
For each foam sample, there are different sets of measurements that are to be repeated in sequence, for the total run duration.

The maximum experiment duration shall be assumed with 24h per experiment run for each sample. At the beginning of a science campaign on orbit replaceable units shall be exchanged (if necessary) and the EC is installed in FSL by the Crew. Each run starts with the foaming process. Data acquisition shall start just at the end of the foaming process. After a run, either the same sample can be processed again, or another sample can be processed.

After a run, data post processing and downlink of results can occur. The results can influence the experiment procedure of subsequent runs, and the possibility to change experiment parameters through telecommand shall be provided. At the end of a science campaign selected scientific data is downlinked and then the EC is uninstalled by the Crew.

Runs Repetition
Each sample shall be tested 3 times (one just needs to “re-foam” the sample after its first period of coarsening).

Experiment Duration and amount of Data
The measurements (alternatively SVS, DWS, DTS, Camera) shall be performed during the whole run duration.
In the following the measurement time is a requirement. On the opposite, the resulting amount of data is based on the required scientific measurements and the specific data production of the instrument, it is an indication but not a requirement.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This experiment might provide useful insights for the manufacture, use and ageing behavior of foams, which are utilized in a wide range of areas, including in cosmetics and personal-hygiene products, in the food industry, in cleaning products, sealing products and for firefighting.
