_source.Title: Constrained Vapor Bubble-2
_source.Keywords: Marangoni flow     Heat pipes
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of CVB-2 is to determine the overall interfacial stability, characterize the hydrodynamics, measure heat transfer coefficients, and determine the overall conductance of a complex fluid (94% Pentane/6% Isohexane) in a microgravity environment.
_source.Approach: The Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment was conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) and the temperature data have been used to analyze the heat transfer mechanisms operating within the quartz cuvette for 40 mm and 30 mm modules. Even with the large millimeter dimensions of the CVB, interfacial forces dominate in these exceedingly small Bond Number systems with small viscous losses. A comparison of the modeling results obtained using a simple one-dimensional analysis of the temperature fields found with the dry and partially liquid pentane filled cuvettes allowed the phase change and radiation fields to be determined in both microgravity and earth gravity. Unique visual observation of the shape of the liquid flow field through a microscope enhanced the understanding of the temperature and vapor pressure [1],[2] measurements. The internal heat transfer processes were very complicated, multidimensional, and the length of the closed system strongly affected the average internal heat transfer processes. Internal radiation was shown to be more significant than originally anticipated as well as the effect of Marangoni convection. The competing processes of capillary flow driving liquid from the cold to the hot end and Marangoni flow driving liquid from the hot end to the cold end resulted in the formation of a central drop and a pinch point in the film thickness profile. The results also indicate that the study of the constrained vapor bubble in an open loop heat pipe configuration would allow the passive bubble more freedom to respond.
_source.Hypothesis: In microgravity environments, the introduction of a higher boiling point, higher surface tension component into a low-boiling-point fluid within a constrained vapor bubble suppresses temperature-induced Marangoni convection, thereby enhancing heat transfer performance and system stability.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Most liquids have a surface tension that decreases as temperature rises. This causes fluid to flow in the direction of higher surface tension, a phenomenon known as Marangoni flow. This reduces the effectiveness of a heat pipe, because liquid cannot return to the hot end. CVB-2 investigates whether a mixture of two fuels (pentane and isohexane) that can reduce Marangoni flow and improve the efficiency of the CVB system on the International Space Station. In addition, the investigation provides insight into how heat transfer functions in microgravity. Most satellites use heat pipes to keep critical parts cool, and improved understanding of fluid mixtures could enable future heat pipes that are smaller, lighter and less expensive to launch. A wide range of high-performance devices must be perpetually cooled in order to function, from supercomputers to personal laptops and LED light bulbs. Fluid mixtures circulating through heat pipes can passively dissipate heat, using less energy than fans or cooling systems. But heat pipe transport systems are sensitive to small differences in temperature, pressure, and gravity. Studying how fluid mixtures and heat pipes function in microgravity provides insight into the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. This also provides insight into how mixtures of fluids behave during boiling, condensation, evaporation, distillation, and stripping. These processes are used in a variety of industries and environmental cleanup.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy 2 Reflight
_source.Keywords: Colloids     Reflight
_source.Objectives:
Sometimes its hard to tell a gas from a liquid. ACE-M2R observes the microscopic behavior of liquids and gases separating from each other.  The investigation examines the behavior of model (colloid rich) liquids and model (colloid poor) gases near the critical point, or the point at which there is no distinct boundary between the two phases.  ACE-M2R uses a new microscope to record micro-scale events on short time scales, while previous experiments observed large-scale behavior over many weeks. Liquids and gases of the same material usually have different densities, so they would behave differently under the influence of gravity, making the microgravity environment of the International Space Station ideal for these experiments.

This investigation is a re-flight of the original ACE-M2 with the intent to resolve issues from the original flight.
_source.Approach: The ACE-M2 investigation utilized 2 Sample Modules (1 is duplicate for back-up) with 15 Sample Wells each for a total of 30 samples, 15 flight and 15 slight identical for back-up. Samples were colloidal fluids varying concentrations of two different types of fluorescent dye and particle size; large and small. Magnetic stir bars embedded in each sample well were used to homogenized each sample. Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
_source.Hypothesis: Near the critical point, variations in density and effective temperature will significantly influence particle interactions, leading to observable changes in phase stability and transition behavior. These changes are expected to reveal underlying mechanisms governing critical phenomena in colloidal systems, enhancing the predictability of particle dynamics in similar environments.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Applications: On Earth, gravity plays a big role in how liquids and gases interact: The heavier liquid phase settles beneath a lighter gas phase, and these differences in density enable easy separation. But the flow and behavior of complex fluids and phase separation where there is little or no gravity is not well understood. A greater understanding of liquid-gas interaction in microgravity could benefit a wide range of fluid storage, transport and processing systems for future spacecraft.
Earth Applications: Particle separation and behavior in liquids, gels, and creams is important for developing consumer and household products, which are worth billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy. Many consumer products are complex fluids, combining microscopic particles in gel or liquid, which are similar to the model colloidal system used in the ACE investigations which give insight into product formulations that could be used to maximize stability and shelf life.

_source.Title: In Space Soldering Investigation
_source.Keywords: In-Space Soldering     Microgravity     surface tension gradient     Welding     porosity     kinematic and dynamic viscosity
_source.Objectives: The primary objective is to better understand the quality of solders in a microgravity environment.  In microgravity, gas bubbles, or void spaces are found in the solder joint and at contact surfaces.  These voids reduce the thermal and electrical conductivity and also provide sites for crack initiation.  Bubbles have less chance to escape in the reduced gravity environment of space. Hence, by designing a systematic series of simple experiments, the objective was to investigate and better understand porosity development, surface wetting, and equilibrium shape formation while soldering in a reduced gravity environment.
_source.Approach: The proposed experiments basically consisted of taking pieces of silver-coated copper wire and bending/twisting them into simple configurations for test coupons. Selected lengths of Kester “44”® 60-40 rosin core solder (5 and 10 cm) were then cut and wrapped around a selected portion of the coupon, to be later melted by heat conduction through the wire using the kit’s soldering iron. A second set of experiments involved feeding 5 and 10 cm lengths of solder onto similar shaped coupons that were being heated by the iron. In principle, the soldering iron was never meant to come in contact with the molten solder. All in all, five soldering sessions were conducted on the ISS that culminated in 86 samples comprising seven different wire configurations, two different solder lengths (5 and 10 cm), and two different melt procedures (conduction melting of wrapped solder and conduction melting of solder being fed onto the wire). The melting experiments took place in the flame retardant Maintenance Work Area, a portable facility in the ISS used to make repairs and conduct other operations in the ISS. A digital camera is placed behind the samples to record the melting and subsequent solidification experiments. Video footage and still pictures were down linked after each experimental session.
_source.Hypothesis: Due to minimized buoyancy in the microgravity environment, it is hypothesized that one would expect additional porosity and enhanced surface tension contributions to porosity shape and mobility. Brazing, soldering, and welding operations in microgravity can be influenced greatly by both wetting and surface tension-driven flows, primary factors in achieving or not achieving a sound joint. For example, processes that rely on gravity-driven separations in the terrestrial environment, such as the removal of gas bubbles from a liquid, may rely on completely different interfacial phenomenon in microgravity.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: An investigation of soldering practices and behavior in a microgravity environment is relevant to our technological needs, particularly with regard to in-space fabrication and repair. The ISSI payload provides unique insight into microgravity soldering methods, which could play a fundamental role in maintaining the International Space Station as well as provide understanding of repair capabilities on future missions to the Moon and to Mars. The study of soldering in space could lead to better soldering techniques here on Earth.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature Control and Gradient Sample 11
_source.Keywords: Colloid     crystallization     rheology     Self-assembly     3D structures     Hard Spheres     temperature gradient
_source.Objectives: ACE-T11 studies the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium with control of particle density, phase and behavior.  Objectives included study of nucleation and growth of crystals within colloidal samples by varying the size and concentration of colloids and depletant, exploring the effect of temperature gradients, and demonstrating control of particle shape and density which is essential for creating high performance materials for 3D printing and advanced optical materials.  The research goal is to produce various colloidal structures and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth. The imaging goal is to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
_source.Approach: The ACE-T11 investigation used 2 Sample Modules (SM), each containing 3 capillary cells for a total of 6 samples. Confocal microscopy was employed for 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids, with phases controlled by adding depletants, adjusting spatial temperature changes, and applying temperature gradients. The size and concentration of both the particles and depletants were varied across different samples. After homogenization using a magnetic stirrer, the particles were left undisturbed to crystallize. Preliminary observations were made with a 2.5X objective, followed by detailed imaging using 10X, 63X, and 100X objectives.
_source.Hypothesis: Under microgravity conditions, colloidal particles would exhibit unique crystallization and self-assembly behaviors that differ from those observed under Earth's gravity. Researchers believed that without the effects of sedimentation, they would better understand the fundamental mechanisms governing colloidal phase transitions and self-organization​.  This hypothesis also included the idea that controlling external factors like temperature and depletant concentration would enable precise manipulation of colloidal structures, allowing for the creation of more complex and functional materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Future space missions will require self-assembly and self-replication technologies for self-repairing materials and devices, essential for long-duration travel. 3D printing and additive manufacturing are crucial for creating replacement parts, with research focusing on developing particle slurries and pastes suited for both micro and regular gravity environments.
This research advances soft matter science, with applications in medicine, electronics, and photonics. Self-assembly techniques will enable new devices for energy and communication, while 3D printing and additive manufacturing rely on optimizing high-density slurries and pastes with diverse mechanical properties.

_source.Title: Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment - II
_source.Keywords: Shearing
_source.Objectives: SHERE-II investigation involves a non-Newtonian fluid that will undergo preshearing (rotation) for a specified period of time, followed by stretching. This combination of shearing and extensional deformations is common in many earth-based polymer processing and manufacturing operations such as extrusion, blow-molding and fiber spinning. However, in order to accurately predict the flow behaviour of polymeric fluids under such deformation histories, an accurate knowledge of the extensional viscosity of a polymer system and its variation with strain rate is critical and will be measured during this experiment. The fundamental understanding and measurement of these complex fluids is important for containerless processing, a key operation for fabrication of parts, such as adhesives or fillers, using elastomeric materials on future exploration missions.
_source.Approach: SHERE-II is designed to investigate the effects of a pre-shear history on the transient extensional viscosity in a uniaxial stretching flow for a model filled viscoelastic suspension (consisting of inert rigid non-Brownian spheres dispersed in a dilute polymer solution).This experiment will generate additional scientific data for dilute viscoelastic polymer solutions in a broad subclass of transient uniaxial extensional flows.Understanding extensional rheology is key in understanding how to process thermoplastic elastomers (flexible elastic polymeric materials), which are very resilient and can be made very thin, and hence, lightweight.Understanding the rheological properties of highly viscoelastic suspensions may be of paramount importance for lunar in-situ resource utilization and for the future construction of a permanent lunar base.SHERE can provide data for engineering design tools that are part of computer-assisted manufacturing (CAM) systems to ensure that the rheological properties of polymeric parts have not been impacted in a variable gravity environment
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates earth-based processing operations. The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character. Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools. This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability. In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites. SHERE plays a role in SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts. In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elastomer films, which are very resilient and can be made thin and lightweight. These elastomeric materials may form the basis of adhesives and fillers utilized in a wide variety of repair applications, especially under a reduced gravity environment, such as the repair of space suits or other similar materials. Understanding and exploiting the ability to fabricate new parts in-situ from a limited number of precursor components is critical in future space missions where weight plays a critical role in the overall cost of a mission. Additionally, in-situ repair provides a means of maintaining systems during transport and during future exploration missions. A fundamental understanding and measurement of the extensional rheology of complex fluids also allows Earth-based manufacturing processes to be controlled and improved. Ground-based work using variants of the Filament Stretching Rheometer includes studies of spinnability, and the investigations of cohesive and adhesive instabilities which manifests themselves in adhesion and tackiness of materials. It has lead to the development of a Resin-spinning technology that allows the formation of ultra-fine elastic threads analogous to spider-silks. Control of the fluid shear history and extensional rheology of test fluid is essential to optimizing the ultimate web properties. Extensional rheology is of critical importance in optimization of polymer processing operations that involve complex flows, i.e. flows that contain both shearing (rotation) and elongation (stretching) components. Suspensions of particles in viscoelastic liquids are used in many terrestrial processing operations: polymer melts with fillers, ceramic pastes, biomedical materials, food, cosmetics or detergents. The final properties of the suspensions are greatly determined by the shape, concentration and size of the filler. In particular, the fillers can range from nanoscopic to microscopic characteristic dimensions, and this leads to very different types of flow behaviors, filler/matrix interactions and dynamics.

_source.Title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
_source.Keywords: fire     Cygnus     SAFFIRE     Smoldering     fire safety     Nomex     SHS     Smoke Distribution
_source.Objectives: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
_source.Approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The Saffire-1I flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, the Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed.  Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked. Details related to samples and experimental parameters are provided in the Experimental Details file in the Science document folder.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The Saffire-II experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

_source.Title: Coarsening in Solid Liquid Mixtures-2
_source.Keywords: Ostwald Ripening     Microgravity     Coarsening     Kinetics
_source.Objectives: The objective of the CSLM-2 investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the addition of higher solid volume percent  samples requiring longer times to reach steady state coarsening rates.
_source.Approach: The CSLM-2 approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM investigation. The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2 were 0.3. 0.5, 0.7, and 0.8.
_source.Hypothesis: The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment, For CSLM-2 it is hypothesized that for large volume fraction solid samples the transient coarsening process will be longer and steady state will be reached much later compared to low volume fraction solid particles.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

_source.Title: Aerosol Sampling Experiment
_source.Keywords: aerosols     Thermophysical properties
_source.Objectives:
Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials. Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air. The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study.

The objectives of ASE were:
1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity.
2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment.
3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions.
4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles.
_source.Approach: The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year).  The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis. The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness.  Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation.
_source.Hypothesis: Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years. There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously. Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled. The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air. This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles. Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity. Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort

_source.Title: Physics of Colloids in Space
_source.Objectives: The primary objectives of the PCS investigation were to successfully grow binary colloidal crystal alloy structures to monitor their nucleation and growth kinetics with static and dynamic light scattering, determine their structures using laser light crystallography and the properties of the superlattices using dynamic light scattering. In addition, the structure and dynamics of gel-like structures formed by colloid-polymer mixtures will be measured using static and dynamic light scattering and the ultimate equilibrium structures behavior of the mixture will be determined. Finally, large scale fractal colloid aggregates and gels will be grown to measure their mechanical properties using dynamic light scattering, and potentially the cell oscillation techniques.
_source.Approach:
For binary colloidal crystal alloy the samples will consist of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) particles, stabilized by a thin coating of poly-12-hydroxystearic acid, and suspended in a mixture of decalin and tetralin adjusted to exactly match the index of refraction of the PMMA. Once in orbit, the samples will be homogenized by rapidly spinning each sample cell and suddenly stopping it. Subsequent to homogenization, the nucleation and growth of the binary colloidal alloy crystallites will be monitored by static light scatter in the forward direction. The small angle light scattering will be complemented by larger angle scattering examining the Bragg reflections of the crystals.
For the colloidal-polymer mixture part of the investigation the colloidal particles will again be PMMA spheres suspended in an index matched fluid.  The volume fractions of these samples will range from about 1% to 30%.  The polymer will be polystyrene, with a molecular weight ranging from about 100,000 to 1,000,000. The colloid-polymer mixtures will be homogenized using the same procedure used for the binary colloid mixtures.  Immediately after they are homogenized, the small angle scattering will be monitored to measure the formation of the gel-like structure. Dynamic light scattering will be performed concurrently as the gel forms to obtain a sensitive indication of the final formation of the gel. Once equilibrium is achieved, if colloidal crystals are formed in one of the phases the growth and structure of the crystals will be studied using both powder average Bragg scattering and dynamic light scattering.
For the fractal colloidal aggregate and gels the aggregation of the colloidal particles will be initiated by mixing the colloidal suspension with another chemical that causes aggregation. Upon initiation of the aggregation, the growth of the colloidal aggregates will be monitored by both dynamic and static light scattering. In addition to the light scattering measurements, small amplitude oscillations of the gel structure will be performed to measure the shear modulus of the gel directly and compare with the light scattering measurements.
_source.Hypothesis: The availability of microgravity will allow binary colloidal superlattices to be formed from different materials providing new insights into the nucleation and growth kinetics of binary colloidal crystal alloy and thereby establish the new field of “colloid engineering.”  This work will unambiguously determine the equilibrium phase diagram for attractive colloidal particles where the attraction is induced by depletion effects through the addition of polymer.  It will also provide important new insight into the transition between equilibrium and kinetically limited behavior, in the absence of sedimentation. Further, this investigation will also lead to the fabrication of fractal colloidal structures that extend over the largest range of length scales ever produced, providing a critical test of our understanding of the formation of these structures.  With such extended structures, it will be possible to study their physical properties and determine the consequences of the scale invariance on the properties. It will determine the fundamental limits of the range over which fractal structures can exist.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The long term goal of this research is to establish a new method of fabricating materials, “Colloid Engineering,” where novel materials are fabricated using colloidal particles as precursors. With appropriate choices of the sizes of the particles, it should be possible to form colloidal alloy crystals of higher volume fraction than can be made with monodisperse particles.  These colloidal alloys may form the precursors for very high quality ceramics.  Alternatively, the particles could be made from different materials, forming colloidal superlattices with novel properties.  Then, for example, one set of particles could be plastic and the other set of particles could be a metal or a semiconductor. Alternatively, these structures may be useful in forming materials with reduced phase space available for radiation, allowing a much simpler way of fabricating structures which possess photonic band gaps. Colloid engineering may offer a simple method for making these materials that completely bypasses the difficulties faced by traditional lithography techniques.  The superlattices could also be used as novel optical switches or displays.

_source.Title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
_source.Keywords: Methane flames     Coflow burner     OH PLIF     Carbon monoxide     Ion-driven Convection     Diffusion Flames     Electric field flames     CO PLIF     Impinging flame     Chemi-ionization
_source.Objectives: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
_source.Approach:
The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution. Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction. There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.
All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR). Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions. Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.
_source.Hypothesis: The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

_source.Title: NASA Research Under Project Quasi-crystalline Undercooled Alloys for Space Investigation (QUASI) and ESA-Based Investigations, THERMOLAB-ISS and ICOPROSOL
_source.Keywords: Nucleation     EML     Supercooling     Thermophysical Properties     QUASI     Batch 1
_source.Proposal Title: NASA Research Under Project Quasi-crystalline Undercooled Alloys for Space Investigation (QUASI) and ESA-Based Investigations, THERMOLAB-ISS and ICOPROSOL
_source.Objectives:
The primary objectives are:
1.  Investigations of nucleation of crystal phases from supercooled (metastable) liquids as a function of stirring (fluid-flow) conditions.   Systematic studies of this under terrestrial conditions are not possible due to the presence of convective flow in the liquid.
2.  Measurements of thermophysical properties of metallic liquids under microgravity conditions, including the specific heat, viscosity, surface tension.  These are then compared with measurements made under terrestrial conditions, when possible.  These data are important for the analysis of the nucleation data, fluid flow calculations; additionally they are important for understanding fundamental connections between liquid dynamics and structure.
_source.Approach: Measurements of the supercooling are made under controlled stirring conditions.  The nucleation rates are derived from the distribution of maximum supercooling following the approach developed by Skripov.   By systematically changing the fluid-flow rates by applying controlled voltages to the heater/positioner coils in the ESA electromagnetic levitation facility on the ISS (ISS-EML), the nucleation rates can be studied as function of stirring, allowing the hypothesis to be examined.
_source.Hypothesis: When the composition of the nucleating crystal phase is different from that of the liquid, long range diffusion can become important for the nucleation process. The potential impact on the nucleation rate depends on the ratio of the attachment rates to the nucleating cluster and the time required for long-range diffusion. This can be investigated by nucleation measurements made as a function of stirring, since fluid-flow can decrease the impact of long-range diffusion.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Realistic modeling approaches have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of materials development. However, progress is frequently hampered by the lack of relevant thermophysical property data needed for the modeling. Further, key processes such as crystal nucleation from the liquid or other phase transitions within the liquid, are often poorly understood, making it difficult to realistically model them. In many cases, the experimental data and a deeper understanding of some processes cannot be obtained from terrestrial experiments due to interactions with sample containers at the temperatures of interest.  The combination of the containerless based terrestrial methods and the ISS-EML enables these measurements.  In addition to their relevance for processes such as additive manufacturing on earth, where nucleation in highly stirred conditions is important, measurements in two different gravitational fields will be important for designing additive manufacturing in space and on the Moon.

_source.Title: An International Space Station Experiment into Fundamental Regolith Processes in Microgravity
_source.Keywords: regolith dynamics     comets     STRATA-1     asteroid     microgravity     Particle Density
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of the Strata-1 investigation was to study the mixing and segregation dynamics of regolith on small bodies by exposing a suite of regolith simulants to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) for a period of one year. In response to variable gravity levels and ambient vibrational environment the Strata-1 experiment aimed to investigate the behavior of regolith simulants specifically chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies.
_source.Approach: The Strata-1 experiment consisted of four evacuated tubes partially filled with regolith simulants.The simulants, namely, glass beads, glass shards, meteorite, and carbonaceous chondrite, were chosen to represent models of regolith covering a range of complexity and tailored to inform and improve computational studies. The four tubes are regularly imaged while moving in response to the ambient vibrational environment using dedicated cameras. The imagery is then downlinked to the Strata-1 science team about every two months. Analyses performed on the imagery includes evaluating the extent of the segregation of Strata-1 samples and comparing the observations to computational models. After Strata-1's return to Earth, x-ray tomography and optical microscopy will be used to study the post-flight simulant distribution. There two simulation methods that have been proposed for this research are the Soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (SSDEM) and the Contact Dynamics Method (CD).
_source.Hypothesis: By utilizing the prolonged microgravity and vibrational conditions of ISS as analogues to those on small Solar System bodies, the Strata-1 investigation aims to answer fundamental questions about how regolith evolves on planetary bodies and what roles particle density, shape, and composition play in the evolution of regolith dynamics.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Strata-1 supports the space exploration program by enabling new interpretation of a wide range of NASA missions including but not limited to Stardust, Deep Impact; EPOXI, Near Earth Asteroid Rendezvous (NEAR), OSIRISREx and Hayabusa-1 and -2. The new Strata information on regolith behavior and mechanics directly assists planning for the Asteroid Redirect Mission ARM), the OSIRIS-REx mission, In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) efforts on small bodies, and upcoming NASA missions to comets and asteroids. The Strata-1 study advances our fundamental understanding of the mechanical behavior of loose material. Results may find utility in any application that involves the mixing of dry materials, such as pharmaceutical tablet manufacture, the study of dune migration and dynamics, and similar fields.

_source.Title: Ring-Sheared Drop - Interfacial Bioprocessing of Pharmaceuticals
_source.Keywords: Drop dynamics     Air-liquid interfaces     Protein Rheology     Biofluids     Non-newtonian Fluid Interfaces     Interfacial Phenomena
_source.Proposal Title: ISS: Collaborative research: Interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals via the ring-sheared drop (RSD) module aboard the ISS
_source.Objectives: The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls. The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface.  Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest.  The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results.  The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity.  Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interfacial shear rate (3, 10, or 30 rpm) on microgravity fluid flow, measured using velocimetry of hollow glass microsphere tracer particles within protein samples.  This campaign intended to confer improved understanding of interfacial protein flows in relation to physiology, the environment, and industry relevant to both spaceflight and Earth.
_source.Approach:
Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls.

Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring.  Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm.  Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI.  ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success.  Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected.  The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS.

Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE. Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration. RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health.
_source.Hypothesis: The study of fluid interfaces coupled to bulk flows, including non-Newtonian response of either the interfacial or the bulk fluid can be uniquely advanced through experimentation in microgravity, where surface tension containment can be achieved at relatively large length scales.  If the hydrodynamics of concentrated protein solutions are precisely measured, then sufficiently descriptive viscosity constitutive relations can be selected or developed from fundamental physics to describe fluid behavior.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Coupled bulk and interfacial flow in the RSD, developed under this grant is currently being analyzed to aid in formulating a model of non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics coupled to a Newtonian bulk flow. These results were recently submitted for publication in a special issue of the journal Fluids, entitled ''Non-Newtonian Flow: Interfacial and Bulk Phenomena.''  While all cases examined remain at least weakly coupled to the bulk flow, this investigation established the effective ranges of model parameters. Bulk flow profiles demonstrate moderate sensitivity of the bulk flow to the behavior of the air-liquid interface, in general increasing with higher Boussinesq number Bq (non-dimensionalized surface viscosity) while maintaining interface to bulk flow coupling. Furthermore, investigation of dissipation may be useful for gauging the interchange between the hydrodynamics and energetics of flow constituents. The change in Bq by the shear-thinning model is indicative of a change in structure of an constituent material. As such, changes in the shape of a constituent of a complex fluid induced by flow are reciprocal with the changes that manifest in flow behavior. Describing the stability of such reciprocal changes could lead to a better understanding of natural systems as well as improved control of transport phenomena.

_source.Title: Capillary Channel Flow - Phase Separation Experiment Unit 2
_source.Keywords: Capillary Channels     CCF     Capillary Flow     Flow Rate     Capillary Channel Flow
_source.Objectives: The objectives are to quantify phase separation efficiency in wedge channels as a function of flow parameters, bubble characteristics, and channel geometry; determine the influence of bubble size and injection frequency on separation efficiency; and optimize wedge geometry for passive phase separation.
_source.Approach: Building upon the CF-CV EU2 approach, the phase separation investigation utilizes a controlled bubble injection system to introduce bubbles of varying sizes and frequencies upstream of the wedge channel. The microgravity environment of the ISS ensures capillary-dominated flow conditions. Systematic variation of bubble injection parameters (size, frequency, location), flow rate, and channel geometry (wedge angle, length) enables comprehensive mapping of phase separation efficiency. High-speed imaging (HSHRC) coupled with wider-view video (MSGC) allows for detailed observation and quantification of bubble migration and coalescence. Image analysis techniques are employed to track bubble trajectories, quantify bubble size distributions before and after the wedge channel, and determine the overall degree of gas-liquid separation. This quantitative data is then correlated with the varied parameters to assess the effectiveness of the wedge geometry for passive phase separation and to optimize design parameters for enhanced performance.
_source.Hypothesis: The hypothesis underlying CCF-PS EU2 is that specific wedge and gapped-wedge channel designs can passively separate liquid and gas phases due to the complex interplay of capillary and inertial forces. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that by carefully adjusting flow conditions, such as flow rate and channel length as well as bubble properties, such as bubble size and frequency, it is possible to identify geometries and regimes suitable for gas-liquid separation, which can be used for spacecraft tank design and liquid supply.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Current spacecraft fuel tanks rely on an additional reservoir to prevent gases from entering the engines during firing. Capillary systems larger than a few millimeters in length are impossible to study on the ground, but the weightlessness on the International Space Station makes research on a variety of capillary channel sizes possible. The results are useful for the design and testing of liquid management systems in current use and for future missions. Rocket fuel tank designs and construction models from space research help to advance new technology and manufacturing capabilities on Earth.

_source.Title: Plant Water Management
_source.Keywords: Root aeration     plant growth     Capillary-driven irrigation     Gas-liquid separation     Passive irrigation systems     Hydroponics     Life-support systems     Controlled-environment agriculture
_source.Proposal Title: Plant Water Management 5 and 6
_source.Objectives:
The primary objectives of the Plant Water Management (PWM) experiments were to:

a) Experimentally characterize and validate the use of passive capillary and  geometric control for plant watering in microgravity.
The research quantified the stability limits of capillary-driven flow under varying conditions, evaluated aeration and bubble management performance within root-zone analogs, and assessed start-up, shutdown, and drainage behaviors of the fluidic system on orbit and also correlated observed flow regimes and saturation levels with computational capillary flow models to improve predictive design tools for reduced-gravity systems.
b) Advance the PWM technology toward higher Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), demonstrating reliable, scalable configurations for integration into future space-based plant growth habitats.
The resulting data and models informed the design of next-generation, low-mass, low-power life-support and food-production systems for long-duration missions on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
_source.Approach: PWM employed passive capillary-based fluidic systems to deliver water and nutrients to plant root zones under microgravity aboard the ISS. Growth modules were designed with controlled channel geometries and surface-wetting properties to direct liquid flow, manage gas-liquid separation, and maintain root-zone aeration. Both hydroponic and soil-based configurations were tested to evaluate performance across different growth media. Measurements included monitoring liquid distribution, root-zone moisture levels, aeration efficiency, and bubble formation, alongside comparing observations to predictive capillary flow models. By systematically varying system geometry, wetting conditions, and operational parameters, the experiments defined design guidelines for robust, low-maintenance plant growth systems for space and analogous terrestrial applications.
_source.Hypothesis: This research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity where gravity-driven fluid behavior is absent, capillary forces, surface tension, and geometric design could provide reliable water and nutrient delivery to plant root zones. Passive physical mechanisms replaced gravity in distributing and reclaiming fluids within the growth systems. Surface-wetting characteristics and channel geometry were designed to maintain root-zone hydration, facilitate aeration, and manage liquid–gas separation without pumps or active components. These mechanisms sustained water availability and oxygen exchange, preventing oversaturation or desiccation. The approach demonstrated that passive capillary systems could support consistent, low-maintenance plant watering and aeration in reduced-gravity environments.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Demonstrating passive fluid management in plant growth systems is enabling reliable water and nutrient delivery in microgravity, supporting long-duration space missions.
Advancing capillary-based irrigation is reducing system mass, complexity, and power requirements. In relation to agriculture on Earth, results from this research are improving precision irrigation, conserving water, and enhancing root-zone aeration in hydroponic and soil systems. Generating validated models of capillary-driven flow is guiding efficient, resilient plant growth technologies. Supporting scalable, low-maintenance systems is fostering innovations in both space life-support and sustainable food production on Earth.

_source.Title: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1
_source.Keywords: USML-1     STDCE-1     thermocapillary flow     buoyancy     Columbia     Surface Tension     Constant Flux     Marangoni Number
_source.Objectives:
The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate:
    -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions.
    -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid.
    -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows.
    -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows
    -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows
_source.Approach:
The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow. This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle.

Theoretical Analysis
   Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S). These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison.

   Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales. This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions.

Numerical Modeling
   Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions. These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation. The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally.

Ground-Based Experiments
   Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects. These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement.

   Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques.

Microgravity Experiments
   Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

Data Analysis and Model Validation
   Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models. This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well.

Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows
Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications.

Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior. These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth.

Technological Advancements
Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics.

Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications. These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance.

Earth-Based Applications
Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale. This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis.

Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications. The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology.

_source.Title: The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides
_source.Keywords: glass     thermophysical properties     viscosity     Electrostatic Levitation Furnace     oxide liquids     density     surface tension     liquid fragility
_source.Objectives:
This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates. These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation.

The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range. Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth. The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration.
_source.Approach:
Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS. Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling.

Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy. Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties.
_source.Hypothesis: Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials. Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them. Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions. We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides. We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation. This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources.

The project was successful on several fronts:
1.	Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples.
2.	First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space.
3.	First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially.
4.	First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing.
5.	Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations.
6.	Two patents are pending based on results of the work. These have a high impact on glass materials processing in space and development of new glass products both on-Earth and in reduced gravity.
7.	The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity.
8.	The results are relevant to the applied research mission of NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) to enable space exploration and utilize materials based on natural resources that are available in space.
9.	Developed and fostered a productive international collaboration.

_source.Title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
_source.Keywords: Soot     Emisssions     Laminar diffusion flames     butane-lighter flame
_source.Objectives:
The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
_source.Approach: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.
_source.Hypothesis: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
(1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments.
(2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions.
(3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation
(4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

_source.Title: Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography
_source.Keywords: Perfect Crystals     lymphoma     Crystallography     Radiation     MnSOD     Cancer     Protein Crystals
_source.Objectives: The Perfect Crystals investigation uses microgravity environment on the International Space Station to grow crystals of human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD). This sheds light on how the antioxidant protein helps protect the human body from oxidizing radiation and oxides created as a byproduct of metabolism. For best results, the analysis technique requires large crystals with minimal imperfections, which are more easily produced in the microgravity environment of the space station.
_source.Approach: The Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography investigation grows perfect, large-volume crystal suitable for neutron macromolecular crystallography of large unit cell protein crystals in microgravity. The protein of study in this investigation is human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD or SOD2), which has an enzymatic mechanism that relies on a proton shuttling pattern that has yet to be fully elucidated. Neutron macromolecular crystallography allows for visualization of protons that cannot be achieved by XRay Diffraction or Cryo-EM, but requires large-volume crystals minimal imperfection for best results. Gravity has been implicated as a cause of defects in crystals grown on Earth. The marriage of the liquid-liquid capillary diffusion crystal growth technique to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) allows for the growth of multiple greater than 1 mm3 crystals with very few defects. Please refer to AccessingPerfectCrystalData.pdf under the Science Documents section.
_source.Hypothesis: In 2001, the Borgstahl laboratory successfully grew large crystals of SOD using microgravity conditions on the International Space Station (ISS). Using existing crystallization hardware that uses the Granada Crystallization Boxes (GCB) for capillary counter diffusion protocols will be used to achieve microgravity crystallization results for SOD. The principal outcome will be to identify the role of hydrogen atoms in enzymatic activity, discern superoxide from peroxide, and water from hydroxide ion by their protonation state and decipher a structure-based mechanism for human MnSOD more precisely than from previous X-ray crystallographic models determined from Earth-grown crystals.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) is implicated in a number of human diseases, including non-Hodgkins lymphoma, lung cancer and colorectal cancer. Understanding how it works is an important step toward developing better prevention and treatment methods for such diseases.
In space application, MnSOD could help researchers protect astronauts on future long-term missions. Astronauts receive significantly more exposure to oxidizing radiation than people on Earth, and on long journeys such as to Mars may receive dangerous doses that create Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS). These can damage DNA and other biomolecules, causing diseases such as cancer. The manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) enzyme converts ROS into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which other enzymes can then break down.  Studies on MnSOD can help researchers can develop artificial techniques to reduce ROS and help protect astronauts on future long-term missions.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 5
_source.Keywords: bijel     Marangoni convection     spinodal decomposition     self assembly     microgravity
_source.Proposal Title: Bijel processing: decoupling the roles of Marangoni and gravitational forces
_source.Objectives: The overarching goal of the project was to gain a better fundamental understanding of the relationship between bijel morphology, rheology, mechanical stability, and processability through combined ground-based and microgravity experiments and theoretical calculations.
_source.Approach: Mixtures of propylene glycol/nitroethane (PG/NE) at their critical composition were prepared. Partially hydrophobic silica particles were suspended in the PG/NE mixture and the suspensions were filled in different cuvettes. On orbit, these cuvettes were heated to 25C, mixed in-situ, and then quenched from 25C to 0C. Following the quench, an imaging protocol was used to collect a stack of 100 images in the Z direction at a spacing of 5 mm.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that interparticle interactions have a profound impact on the rheology of bijel particulate suspensions and attempts to answer the fundamental scientific question as to how the various forces at the colloidal scale are affected by Marangoni convection in microgravity. The nature of interparticle interactions and its impact on rheology has profound implications for the processability of bijels and the ability to transform them into functional materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The ability to design and fabricate the unique 3-dimensional bijel structures opens a wide spectrum of new structures for applications that can benefit from synthesis of hierarchically
porous monoliths and composites with a spinodal-like microstructure in which every constituent phase is naturally continuous throughout the entire sample volume. This type of tailored porous
microstructures can improve the physical properties and performance of materials used in a number of space and terrestrial applications. Space exploration applications include improved energy
storage batteries and fuel cells, and catalytic microreactors for lower mass and volume designs in spacecraft life support and ISRU systems. There is a diverse array of potential terrestrial applications in electrochemical energy conversion and storage, tissue engineering, sensing, microstructured composites with optimized mechanical properties for MEMS, microfluidic heat exchangers and catalytic reformers, separations.

_source.Title: Fabrication of Amorphous Metals in Space
_source.Keywords: bulk metallic glass composites     metallic glass forming alloys     dendritic morphology     composition profile
_source.Objectives:
The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG). Specific questions to be answered were:

   (a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity?
   (b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix?
   (c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity?
   (d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix?
   (e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases?
_source.Approach: The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter). The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders. The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation. On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack. They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout. The samples were then  cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition. The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity.
_source.Hypothesis:
The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid. In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form. Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity.

On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning:
(a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales
(b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms)
(c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed.

In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion. For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case. After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained. It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The development of innovative new materials is a fundamental part of future terrestrial and space technologies. These materials have a tremendous benefit towards improving life on Earth, from improving the accessibility and cost of solar power, to making cars safer and stronger, to reducing the mass of aircraft, for example. Innovative technologies typically require new materials tailored for those applications. This drives materials development.
