_source.Title: Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules
_source.Keywords: InSb     Baffle     Semiconductor Crystals     Segregation     Microgravity     Directional Solidification     Magnetic Field     Bridgman Configuration
_source.Objectives: There are both technology demonstration objectives and scientific objectives. The technology demonstration objectives are to test the performance of an automatically moving baffle in microgravity and to determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.The science objectives are to visualize the melt/encapsulant behavior in microgravity and to grow doped InSb without dewetting. The key goal of SUBSA was to clarify the origin of the melt convection in space and to reduce the magnitude to the point that it does not interfere with the transport phenomena.
_source.Approach: In the space environment, accelerations produce circular motions that affect the solidification of crystal growth/semiconductor materials flight experiments, resulting in a material that is less useful.The objectives of SUBSA are:Test the performance of an automatically moving baffle (used to minimize melt motion).Visualization of the melting process to identify what causes the melt motion.Production of several crystals with reproducible properties.To determine the behavior and possible advantages of liquid encapsulation in microgravity conditions.
_source.Hypothesis: A baffle placed inside a melt reduces the effective size of the melt and leads to a decrease in the amount of convection. The combined effect of microgravity (reduction of gravitational acceleration by a factor of 10^6 ) and a small zone melt (reduction of the size and temperature differential by a factor of 10^3 ) will generate the effective conditions of “nano-gravity” (the Rayleigh number will be reduced by a factor of 10^9 ).
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The SUBSA furnace, with its capability to control and visualize melting and solidification of semiconductor crystals has increased our understanding of semiconductor crystal growth phenomena. The transparent furnace coupled with the video downlink and real-time commanding capability provided a powerful tool for scientists to watch the motion of the crystal-melt interface as semiconductor crystals were formed. The design of the SUBSA ampoule which includes a baffle and a system that prevents de-wetting resulted in crystals whose properties have not been disrupted by micro-accelerations at the Station, making it possible for future researchers to produce the high-quality semiconductor crystals that are in demand on Earth.

_source.Title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
_source.Keywords: microgravity     ACME CLD Flame     Fuels     laminar diffusion flames     Combustion Integrated Rack     Flames
_source.Proposal Title: Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment
_source.Objectives:
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.
_source.Approach: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.

_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.

_source.Title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

Person.First Name: John L de Peter James Dennis

_source.Keywords: Buoyancy     Diffusion Flames     Fire Safety     Heat Flux     Radiative Extinction     Polymer     ACME     Extinction Limit     Flammability     Modeling     Triple Flame
_source.Proposal Title: Experimental Investigation of Emulated Burning Rate at Various Gravity Levels
_source.Objectives:
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
  1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25  and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
  2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
  3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
_source.Approach:
To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests.

For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared.

The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions.

In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions.

We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.
_source.Hypothesis:
The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials.

The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

_source.Title: Capillary Flow Experiment
_source.Keywords: Capillary Flow Experiment (CFE)     Capillary forces     CFE
_source.Objectives:
1. The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances.
2. The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers. Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners.
3. The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap. A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena.
_source.Approach: Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft.
_source.Hypothesis: The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions. This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability. The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems. By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity. These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe. The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing).

_source.Title: IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions
_source.Keywords: water treatment     medical equipment     fluid flow
_source.Objectives: The main goal of this experiment is to demonstrate in a space environment, a prototype system that produces USP grade SWI, and mixes the SWI with sterile USP sodium chloride to produce a homogeneous Normal Saline IV fluid. The experiment shall also demonstrate at least one bubble removal apparatus, as this is a critical step to prevent delivering harmful gas emboli to patients when the deployed system is used. The system will utilize a single flow rate, determined by the maximum volume/hour required for a worst-case-scenario medical event.
_source.Approach:
The IVGEN investigation employs a comprehensive and well-structured approach to demonstrate and validate the feasibility of producing IV fluids in space. The approach encompasses a combination of on-orbit experimentation, ground-based testing, and meticulous data analysis, as summarized below:

 On-Orbit Experimentation: The core of the investigation involves a flight experiment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), utilizing a prototype IV fluid generation system. This experiment simulates the conditions and constraints of a space mission, allowing for direct testing of the system's performance in a microgravity environment.

 Ground-Based Testing: Prior to the flight experiment, a rigorous ground-based test program is conducted to:
    -Concept Verification: Validate the design and performance of key system components, such as the bubble separators and mixers, in both normal and reduced gravity environments.
    -Input Water Analysis: Characterize the quality of potential water sources, including ISS potable water and various CEV water sources, to ensure the system's compatibility and effectiveness.
    -Temperature Effects: Assess the impact of varying temperatures on the system's performance, particularly on the DI cartridge and the conductivity sensors.

 Data Acquisition and Analysis: During the on-orbit experiment, a comprehensive dataset is collected, including:
    -Environmental Data: Temperature, pressure, and acceleration measurements to understand the system's operating environment and potential impact on performance.
    -System Performance Data: Conductivity, flow rate, and image data to assess the purification, mixing, and bubble removal processes.

 Post-Flight Sample Analysis: The two 1.5-liter bags of NS produced on orbit are returned to Earth for rigorous testing by a certified laboratory, ensuring the produced IV fluid meets USP standards.

 Data Interpretation and Scaling: The collected data is meticulously analyzed to:
    -Validate System Performance: Confirm the successful production of USP-compliant NS solution in microgravity.
    -Identify Challenges and Limitations: Assess potential issues and areas for improvement based on observed system behavior.
    -Enable System Scaling: Utilize the data to inform the design and development of a larger, operational system capable of meeting the needs of future exploration missions.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that a prototype system, utilizing deionization, magnetic stirring, and bubble separation techniques, can effectively produce USP-compliant normal saline solution from readily available spacecraft potable water sources in a microgravity environment.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Due to mass and volume limitations, space vehicles cannot carry sufficient IV fluid for medical contingencies. A filtering and mixing system that can make IV fluid in situ would provide the treatment capability without the mass and volume constraints. IVGEN was designed and will be tested to meet that need. IVGEN technology could be used on Earth to generate IV fluid in Third World countries where medical resources are limited.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Imaging, Folding and Assembly of Colloidal Molecules
_source.Keywords: metallodielectric Janus spheres     lock-and-key particles     microscopy imaging     electric-field cell
_source.Objectives: In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction). In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions. Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy. We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation.
_source.Approach: The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres. For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes. For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter). The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron. For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching.
_source.Hypothesis: In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations. Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants. This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure. With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space. Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature. Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials. The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well. Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality. They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles. As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment-Nanoparticle Haloing
_source.Keywords: Nanoparticle haloing     microfluids     self-assembly     NPH     colloids     microscopy
_source.Proposal Title: Influence of Gravity on Electrokinetic and Electrochemical Colloidal Self-Assembly for Future Materials
_source.Sponsoring Agency: Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR)  NASA
_source.Objectives:
Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently.  In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles.  To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles.

The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions:
   • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity?
   • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed?
   • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals?
   • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation?
_source.Approach:
The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments.

Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera.

ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells. Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary.
1- Short mix of sample.
2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample.
3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI).
4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging.
5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits.
6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.
_source.Hypothesis: When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures. Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles. Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle.  Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape. Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects. Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.

_source.Title: Gradient Driven Fluctuation Experiment
_source.Keywords: non-equilibrium fluids     Foton-M3     Gradient-driven fluctuations     GRADFLEX
_source.Objectives:
The primary objectives of the GRADFLEX investigation can be summarized as follows:

To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced.

To measure the divergence of large-size fluctuations by observing and quantifying this divergence up to the limits imposed by the sample size.

To quantify the amplitude and spatial extent of fluctuations by precisely measuring the mean-squared amplitude of the fluctuations as a function of both wave vector (spatial extent) and frequency (temporal dynamics).

 The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity.

Beyond the static properties (amplitude and spatial extent), the investigation also seeks to characterize the temporal dynamics of the fluctuations.
_source.Approach: The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus. Two fluid systems (CS₂ and polystyrene/toluene) were subjected to precisely controlled temperature gradients. Quantitative shadowgraphy, a sensitive optical technique, measured both static (S(q)) and dynamic (S(q,ω)) properties of the fluctuations, with images acquired at specific rates for each. Data analysis involved Fourier transforms and spectral techniques to extract fluctuation amplitudes and dynamics and to address unexpected noise. The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments. The approach combined and refined a sophisticated design, enabling robust testing.
_source.Hypothesis: In the absence of gravity, thermally-driven fluctuations in a fluid subjected to a temperature gradient will exhibit significantly enhanced amplitude and spatial extent, with their mean-squared amplitude diverging with the size of the fluctuation and exhibiting altered dynamics up to the limits imposed by the sample dimensions.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Throughout the course of this work it has been necessary to constantly improve the experimental method of choice, namely the quantitative shadowgraph. This development has now reached the stage where it is clear that this method, if handled properly, represents a viable method of carrying out both dynamic and static light scattering at scattering angles so small as to defy the imagination of of anyone who has worked in the field. Although it is likely to take some time for the knowledge we have gained to be disseminated, there is no reason this method cannot be added to the scattering arsenal. Furthermore, it can also be applied to X-rays, enabling one to extend the lower limit of X-ray scattering as well. The consequences of putting a new technique into the hands of researchers is difficult to asses in advance. Basically, however, this method will enable quantitative measurements of various systems having size ranges that are too large for existing techniques. Obvious examples are the crystallization process in colloidal systems, gelation processes, and aggregation and flocculation. Because scattering provides excellent statistical averages, the method should prove quite complementary to visualization techniques such as microscopy.

_source.Title: Observation and Analysis of Smectic Islands in Space

Person.Last Name: Glaser Maclennan Stannarius Clark Hall Tin
Person.First Name: Matthew Joseph Ralf Noel Nancy Padetha

_source.Objectives:
OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands. Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes. The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal.
The specific research objectives are:
    -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics.
    -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence
_source.Approach: The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity. OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals. The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids. Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays. It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices.
_source.Hypothesis: In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them. Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal. Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times. It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam.

_source.Title: Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification
_source.Keywords: Microgravity     Diffusion controlled crystal growth     Porosity     MICS     Hydration     Cement Solidification     Density     Cement
_source.Proposal Title: Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification (MICS)
_source.Objectives: The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the complex process of cement solidification by conducting experiments in the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and further the development of an in-situ lunar concrete material.
_source.Approach: Several different mixture combinations of tricalcium aluminate (C3A), tricalcium silicate (C3S), ordinary portland cement (OPC), superplasticizer (SP) and ratios of cement to water were packed in commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with separate compartments divided by an internal, burstable seal which allowed mixing of materials under sealed conditions in microgravity and terrestrial conditions. Space and ground samples were mixed simultaneously and at the same conditions of 20 ºC ± 2 ºC, 1 ATM and 35% RH. As such, gravity is considered the only variable between the space and ground experiments. After a specific period of hydration samples were subjected to a wide variety of characterization techniques such as image analysis and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) to assess porosity and pore size distribution, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to estimate degree of hydration, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA) for compositional analysis. Phase distribution, pore structures, and crystal morphology as a function of composition and gravity level was documented.
_source.Hypothesis: The research hypothesis for the ISS experiments is that minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena, such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection results in a purely diffusion-controlled hydration process. Without the physical effects induced by gravity, diffusion will lead to a more uniform distribution of phases. As such, the dissolving cement particles will disperse in the aqueous solution, resulting in greater uniformity of features such as pore structures and crystal morphology in the hardened cement matrix. A different microstructure is expected to form in microgravity (µg), which possibly leads to different physical properties of µg-hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emissions.

_source.Title: Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures
_source.Keywords: Ostwald Ripening     Microgravity     coarsening     kinetics
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of the microgravity experiment was to measure the temporal evolution of the average size-scale of a solid-liquid mixture during solidification. Specifically, the objective was to measure the average intercept length and the average section area of the solid particles at various times and for various volume fractions of solid. Using this data the amplitude of the temporal power law for the average section area. and intercept length was to be determined. Once the amplitude of the temporal power law is known, the objective is to compare the result to the theoretical predictions on the dependence of the amplitude of the power law on the volume fraction of the coarsening phase. The objective was also to determine the steady-state particle size distribution by measuring the distribution of section area of of the particles in a plane and the intercept length distribution.
_source.Approach: The sample holder in the Sample Processing Unit (SPU) contained four Lead-Tin samples of 12 mm diameter and 6 mm thickness for various volume fractions of Tin. The SPU heated the samples up to 185 degree C in less than 9.5 min, held the temperature for a predetermined time at 185 ± 0.1 degree C ranging from 0.25 to 48hrs (coarsening phase).  The heating system consists of two disc resistance heaters and one ring heater to insure uniform heating with four resistance temperature devices (RTD) installed mid-way between the discs 1 to measure temperature of the samples. Subsequent to the predetermined coarsening time the samples were quenched using pressurized air to nearly room temperature in approximately 1 minute. Once the samples were returned to earth they were sectioned and the measurements of particle size and distribution was performed.
_source.Hypothesis: The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time. The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The importance of coarsening from a commercial perspective arises from the major effect that coarsening has on the properties of materials, for example materials can become stronger while undergoing coarsening.  The CSLM experiment will assess the validity of the theory of coarsening that has been used to design materials. The result will be a more rational design of materials using a first-principles approach, reduced development cost for the production of new materials and better materials properties.  Such a first-principles design of materials will enable NASA and industry to create materials in a rapid cost-efficient manner with the superior properties that are needed for space exploration.

_source.Title: Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification - Multi-use Variable Gravity Platform
_source.Keywords: tricalcium aluminate     cement     variable gravity     gypsum     hydration
_source.Objectives:
The purpose of the MICS-MVP is to investigate and understand the complex process of cement solidification as a function of variable gravity and to advance the use of
concrete materials for extraterrestrial infrastructure. MICS-MVP will identify the differences between the hydration reaction and microstructural formation at the different gravity levels.
_source.Approach:
Two different mixture combinations of with water and gypsum and tricalcium silicate (C3S) with water were hydrated under 5 different gravity levels, namely, Earth's
gravity, microgravity, and simulated gravity levels of the Moon, Mars, and a statistical point at 0.7g.  The different components were each placed in opposing compartments of a plastic pouch and separated by a middle burstable seal. To burst the seal, the water filled compartment was rolled up from the outside edge towards the middle until enough forward pressure was achieved to burst the seal. The water is then completely moved into the compartment containing the tricalcium aluminate (C3A) or tricalcium silicate (C3S) and the paste is mixed by a rubber spatula and/or kneaded by hand to reach a homogeneous state. A plastic clip is then attached to help consolidate the paste at one end of the pouch. This mixing procedure generally took a few minutes per sample. The ISS itself provides a microgravity environment, whereas the gravity levels of extraterrestrial bodies that are less than Earths were simulated with centrifugal forces within the Multi-use Variable-gravity Platform (MVP). Samples at different gravity levels were hydrated for different lengths of time, following which the centrifuge was shut off and the samples continued to hydrate till they were returned to earth. The samples were characterized for pore size, pore distribution, portlandite size distribution, crystal morphology, and phase content.
_source.Hypothesis:
It is hypothesized that under variable reduced gravity conditions different transport phenomena such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection are minimized and a
more diffusion dominant transport will lead to varying degree of uniformity in distribution ofphases, porosity, and crystal morphology. A different microstructure is expected  to form in at different gravity levels which possibly leads to different physical properties of the reduced gravity hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew. Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties. Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties. Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emission.

_source.Keywords: Colloids     Microgravity     Polymers
_source.Objectives:
The goal of the BCAT investigations is to further investigate critical, fundamental problems in colloid science and evolve the field of ‘colloid engineering’, which creates materials with novel properties using colloidal particles as precursors.  The BCAT-5 investigation had four primary objectives corresponding to specific samples:
Phase Seperation (BCAT-5-PhaseSep): to study collapse (phase separation rates that impact product shelf-life).
Compete (BCAT-5-Compete): to study the competition between phase separation and crystallization, which is important in the manufacture of plastics and other materials.
Seeded Growth (BCAT-5-SeededGrowth): to study the properties of concentrated systems of small particles when 99.8% are identical 0.36 diameter micron spheres and 0.2% are 4.14 microns in diameter (11.5x larger); these seed particles may cause heterogeneous crystal growth.
3D Melt (BCAT-5-3D-Melt): to study the mechanisms of crystal formation and 3D melting using colloidal particles that change size with temperature.
_source.Approach: BCAT is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS.  The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in cuvettes in individual wells.  The samples were manually homogenized using a stir bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each cuvette.  Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using EarthKAM, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.
_source.Hypothesis: Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth.  This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Insights from BCAT-5 enhance the design of colloidal products critical to space missions, such as food and consumables. The Phase Separation component investigates multi-phase interactions with potential applications in liquid waste recycling, coolant systems, and rocket fuel flow control. By manipulating crystal size during production, BCAT-5 aims to create stronger, more durable materials with extended shelf lives for both terrestrial and extraterrestrial use. Additionally, BCAT-5 advances colloidal engineering by studying how crystallization interacts with phase separation, a key factor in improving consumer and industrial products. Findings help reduce manufacturing defects in colloid-based materials, like plastics, and optimize household goods, such as fabric softeners, by minimizing costly additives. The experiment also supports breakthroughs in next-generation technologies, including advanced optics, medical tools, and smart materials. The Seeded Growth component examines how larger seed particles influence crystal size, enabling better control in producing ceramics, optical filters, and composite materials while refining predictive computer models for crystal formation.

_source.Title: Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-1
_source.Keywords: Protein Crystallization     Molecular Transport     Crystal Growth Rate Dispersion     Advanced Photon Source (APS)     Microgravity     Synchrotron Radiation     x-ray diffraction     Macromolecular Crystals
_source.Proposal Title: Effect of Macromolecular Transport on Microgravity Protein Crystallization
_source.Objectives:
Specific objectives of this investigation were
1. On the ISS and concurrently in earth control experiments, compare incorporation of protein aggregates (monomers versus dimers, trimers, etc.) into growing protein crystals. Detection of aggregates in the crystal will be qualitatively assessed via LMM’s and laboratory fluorescence confocal microscopes and quantitatively measured using mass spectrometry (ion spray and/or MALDI). Based on the percentage incorporation of larger aggregates within the crystal, the effect of molecular filtering based on differences in diffusion rates will be assessed.
2. Measure crystal growth rates in 1g versus μg for different size aggregates of proteins with molecular weights ranging from less than 20kDa to more than 1,200kDa.
3. Compare the defect density and crystal quality via mass spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction quality of crystals grown at different rates in a 1g environment.
_source.Approach: A total of four cassettes were sent to the ISS, containing eight samples each. Each sample could contain either; (1) Lysozyme, (2) pfGST, (3) BSA, or (4) XptA1. For each protein investigated, preparative size exclusion chromatography (SEC) was used to fractionate protein monomers from the naturally occurring protein aggregates. The aggregates were then segmented into small, medium, and large categories. Fluorophores (excitation wavelengths: 594 and 488) were chosen and attached to the macromolecules, producing a bright fluorescent signal (red and green) and each exhibited a slow photo-bleach so that fluorescence was maintained for the duration of the proposed crystallization experiments. The samples were upmassed frozen at -80C and thawed to ambient temperature (~20C). After thawing nucleation of the proteins were observable within 24 – 96 hours. Observations were conducted with a confocal fluorescent microscope where the total fluorescence observed for each crystal (after normalizing for the different crystal volumes) provides an estimation of the relative amount(s) of aggregated (containing the fluorophore) versus monomeric (no fluorophore) protein incorporated within the growing crystal.
_source.Hypothesis:
This investigation addresses the hypothesis that improved quality of microgravity-grown protein crystals is the result of two macromolecular characteristics that exist in a buoyancy-free, diffusion-dominated solution:
• Slower crystal growth rates, due to slower protein transport to the growing crystal surface
• Predilection of growing crystals to incorporate protein monomers versus higher protein aggregates due to differences in transport rates
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Using three-dimensional protein structure information, researchers can determine how proteins function and in cases where these proteins are involved in disease processes, the structure is often used to design new drugs that specifically interact with the protein. Many leading drugs today are the product of structure-based drug design. While enormous strides have been made in the last decade, there remain a large number of important proteins where the difficulty of obtaining crystals of sufficient quality is the chief barrier to their structural analysis. The impact of this investigation is for one important class of proteins, membrane proteins, comprises a number of targets identified by the pharmaceutical industry as high-value commercial opportunities (membrane proteins were the targets for approximately 67% of all past marketed drugs and it is estimated that they will comprise targets for an equal percentage of all future drugs). Membrane protein crystallization represents one area where the onset of space commercialization can maximize the impact of the microgravity environment in space-based research applications for the academic, government and pharmaceutical industries. Other areas include high-value aqueous proteins and protein complexes (based on their functional importance in biological systems) many of which yield crystals of poor quality under 1g laboratory conditions. Access to unique data optimized in microgravity could have great relevance for understanding protein structures and advancing new drugs into the pharmaceutical market.

_source.Title: Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics
_source.Keywords: immiscible alloys     Interfacial Stability     Microgravity     hypermonotectic     Coupled Growth
_source.Objectives: The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems. Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system.
_source.Approach:
The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996. Processing conditions
were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples. The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys. Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing. Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission. A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s. Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation aimed to answer fundamental unanswered questions concerning solidification of immiscible alloys, namely: (a) is it possible to solidify a hypermonotectic alloy under steady state interfacially stable conditions to produce a fibrous microstructure, (b) can a simple supercooling approach predict stability limits, (c) does extensive diffusion in the liquid phases result in morphological effects not observed in eutectic systems, and (d) what role does surface tension driven flow play at the solidification front.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Many alloys in immiscible systems show great promise for potential applications in areas that include superconductors, magnetic materials, catalysts, and electrical contacts. For example, some immiscible alloys may be used to produce filters that can remove micron-sized particles for medical applications. Other alloys are expected to exhibit superconducting characteristics or have unusual magnetic properties.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Aging Dynamics and Stress-Relaxation in Colloidal Gels Studied in Microgravity
_source.Keywords: Critical Casimir Force     Consolution Curve     polymers     Photon correlation spectroscopy     rheology     Growth kinetics     CCF     Gels     creep     jamming     Gelation
_source.Objectives:
Colloidal stability is critical to soft matter systems, especially to consumer products. These structures change in time, by processes know as coarsening - meaning the spacing between particles compact. This compaction continually changes this structure. When the structures created in the products can longer resist the gravitational stresses (e.g. buoyancy) on the structures, they collapse. The collapse, such as those that occur in geological formations during earthquakes, is often abrupt and without warning (delayed collapse). This is the essence of product instability. For some systems, the gel collapse can be anticipated by precursors, that can potentially be detected and forecasted.

This research will have significant impacts in two areas:
     •	It is not clear how the microscopic structure and its dynamics are related to the gel mechanical properties. The structure evolution controls the aging of the gel, and, on earth, this eventually leads to collapse. This work may significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science.
     •	Second, relaxation of localized stresses in an amorphous solid brought by a rapid solidification process is ubiquitous in nature and can damage and destroy the materials. Besides affecting the rheological properties of the materials, these dynamics rule the aging of the thermal systems at rest. The detection of failure precursors, as the ones discovered in our colloidal gel, can potentially allow us to forecast the material failure before catastrophic rupture.
_source.Approach:
The ACE-T10 experiment exploited the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). The Light Microscopy Module (LMM) is an automated microscope. It permitted flexible imaging (e.g., bright field, dark field, phase contrast, confocal microscopy) for physics experiments and can be controlled remotely from the ground. The LMM accommodated sample change-out and fluid containment and included a glove box for on-orbit sample manipulation.

The ACE-T10 experiment used include confocal microscopy, which utilized a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera. A sample’s three-dimensional crystal structure can thus be reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program. This information, in turn, enabled the observation and measurement of the colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics. The confocal module was attached and aligned to the side of the LMM. The microscope used a reflecting mirror to direct the light to and from the sample.

ACE-T10 utilized 6 capillary cells in 2 holding modules. The capillary cells, each contained about 20 microliters of the sample fluid and a magnetic stainless steel stir bar. Samples were stirred prior to example. The sample temperature was adjusted between 20 – 60 °C in order to find the transition temperature where the sample became a gel.
_source.Hypothesis: ACE-T10 delivered unique insights into the restructuring behavior of thermo-reversible colloidal gels, a topic of noticeable interest for the community of scientists dealing with soft materials. In normal gravity experiments, the ACE-T10 science team found evidence that the aging of these soft gels proceed via a sequence of sudden intermittent bursts of dynamical activity that resembles the ‘critical avalanche’ phenomena observed in several driven systems. The evidence collected suggests that, in a soft solid, these avalanches may be triggered by thermal agitation and occur spontaneously, even in the absence of other external forces. However, because of the density difference between the fluid and the particles in the gel network, gravity may play a role as well. Performing the ACE-T10 experiment in microgravity provided a unique opportunity to determine the gravity contribution.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Earth benefits/spin-off applications include understanding the behavior of weak gels and their aging can help materials scientists to make consumer product with longer shelf lives. In addition, because several features of the failure dynamics of disordered materials are system independent,  the results obtained using this model colloidal system can be generalized to other materials. This potentially can help to develop new way to characterize aging material and suggest their replacement before catastrophic failure.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment -Temperature controlled- 2
_source.Keywords: Critical Casimir attraction     Complex crystallisation kinetics     Electrostatic repulsion
_source.Proposal Title: Assembly of Colloidal Superstructures by Critical Casimir Forces in Microgravity
_source.Sponsoring Agency: European Space Agency (ESA)  Netherlands Organization for Applied Scientific Research (TNO)
_source.Objectives:
The objective of this experiment is the investigation of the assembly of complex structures from micron-scale colloidal particles interacting via tunable attractive interactions. Regulating temperature enables control of particle interactions.

This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent).  In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

By studying this process based on critical Casimir forces in microgravity, where sedimentation and convection are essentially removed, we will learn how to adjust complex attractive particle interactions. This simple reversible process is controlled by adjusting the size of the tunable temperature fluctuations in a two-component fluid (solvent).  In principle, the ingredients are simple: particles suspended in a binary solvent, without the addition of any other components.

Understanding self-assembly processes like the critical Casimir effect will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of temperature-controlled super structure assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes.
_source.Approach:
The ACE-T2 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM). Accordingly, the ACE-T2 experiment will use a camera which scans at 30 frames per second of confocal images. ACE-T2 utilizes capillary cells. Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary.
1- Short mix of sample.
2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample.
3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI).
4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging.
5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits.
6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.
_source.Hypothesis: The critical Casimir effect is affected by temperature, particle size and relative concentrations and will impact the growth of complex nanostructured materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Understanding self-assembly processes will teach ways to grow complex nanostructured materials. Furthermore, these experiments will provide fundamental insight into the nature of self-assembly, the relation between complex interactions and complex equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures, and the dynamics of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium growth processes. Ultimately, it is hoped that these insights can be applied to advances in in photonic and optoelectronic technologies.

_source.Objectives:
The TEMPUS (Tiegelfreies ElektroMagnetisches Prozessieren Unter Schwerelosgkeit) facility is a research instrument designed to perform electromagnetic levitation studies in reduced gravity. TEMPUS was a joint undertaking between DARA, the German space agency, and the Microgravity Science and Applications Division of NASA. Specific objectives for the different investigations carried out by US Principal Investigators using this facility is categorized by different classes:
Class A: Studies of undercooling phenomena and the kinetics of nucleation (Prof. M. Flemings, MIT, Prof. R. Bayuzick, Vanderbilt Univ), Class B: Measurement of specific heat in liquid metals using an AC calorimetry technique (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH), Class C: Measurement of viscosity and surface tension of undercooled metals (Prof. J. Szkeley, Prof. M. Flemings, MIT), Class D: Measurement of thermal expansion in undercooled materials (Prof W. Johnson, CALTECH).
In addition to the US Principal Investigators, available data from European investigations performed on TEMPUS and captured here include Viscosity and Surface Tension of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermophysical Properties of Undercooled Metallic Melts (Dr. Egry, DLR, Germany), Thermal Expansion of Glass forming Metallic Alloys in the Undercooled State (Dr. Samwer, Georg-August-Universitat Gottingen, Germany), and Thermodynamics and Glass Formation Undercooled Liquid Alloys (Dr. Wunderlich and Dr. Fecht, University of Ulm, Germany).
_source.Approach: Metallic samples of 7 or 8 mm diameter are positioned in the TEMPUS coils by electromagnetic forces and melted by induced currents. A ''squeezing'' force is then applied to a stably positioned liquid sample to induce oscillations. The rate of decay of the amplitude of these oscillations can be observed in order to measure the viscosity at different temperatures, while the frequency of the oscillation modes is used to deduce the surface tension at these temperatures. Measurements are planned on reactive, refractory melts (Zr), high-viscosity eutectics (ZrNi, PdSi), and industrial alloys (Fe-Cr-Ni) in addition to standard materials for comparison (Au, Ni). In addition, mathematical modeling designed to give a detailed understanding of what can be expected from prevailing conditions in the flight experiments was also developed.
_source.Hypothesis: Levitation, positioning and processing of materials which are not in direct contact with container surfaces, provides a unique opportunity to study a number of phenomena. In particular, the lack of contact with container walls reduces the possibility for heterogeneous nucleation in studies of the processing of molten materials. The study of the properties and solidification of undercooled materials is facilitated by containerless processing.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The accurate determination of the thermophysical properties of liquid materials is important for fundamental and practical reasons, including verification of atomistic models of the liquid state, nucleation studies of phase transition, and modeling of materials processing operations. In addition, these studies often focus on advanced materials such as metallic glass forming materials. Metallic glasses are an industrially important new class of materials. They are ductile, isotropic and corrosion resistant and are used in magnetic storage media films.
